articles.body_html:
Angular applications rarely stay small forever.

A project starts with a single application, a few components, and some services. Over time, new requirements appear. Another application is introduced. Teams start sharing components, models, and utilities.

Eventually, someone suggests:

"We should move everything into a monorepo and use Nx."

And honestly, that might be a good idea.

But is it always necessary?

Angular CLI already supports multiple projects in a workspace. Nx adds powerful capabilities for dependency management, task execution, caching, and CI optimization, but those capabilities come with additional concepts and tooling.

So, when does Nx actually make sense?

Rather than simply explaining what a monorepo is, I want to explore this through a practical example, compare Angular CLI with Nx, and understand what changes when a workspace grows.

The goal isn't to prove that Nx is better.

The goal is to understand when the benefits of Nx justify its additional complexity.

1. First, What Problem Are We Trying to Solve?

Let's imagine a company with two Angular applications:

  • An administrative dashboard.
  • A customer portal.

Both applications display information about vehicles, appointments, and operational status.

Initially, they are completely independent.

company/
├── admin-app/
└── customer-app/

Each application has its own dependencies, configuration, and deployment pipeline.

This is a perfectly reasonable architecture.

However, the applications eventually start sharing code:

  • UI components.
  • Domain models.
  • API clients.
  • Validation utilities.
  • Design system elements.

Now we have a few options:

  1. Duplicate the code.
  2. Create an internal npm package.
  3. Share code through a monorepo.
  4. Introduce a workspace tool such as Nx.

The important distinction is that sharing code and sharing a repository are two different decisions.

A shared npm package can work perfectly well across separate repositories. A monorepo becomes particularly interesting when applications need to coordinate their dependencies, development, testing, and releases.

Before introducing a new tool, we should understand which problem we are actually solving.

2. Angular CLI Already Supports Monorepos

This is something that is sometimes overlooked.

Angular CLI is not limited to a single application per repository.

It supports workspaces containing multiple applications and libraries.

Let's create one.

Creating an Angular workspace 

ng new company-platform --no-create-application

cd company-platform

Now we can generate multiple applications:

ng generate application admin

ng generate application customer

And shared libraries:

ng generate library shared-ui

ng generate library shared-data

Our workspace now looks something like this:

company-platform/
├── projects/
│   ├── admin/
│   ├── customer/
│   ├── shared-ui/
│   └── shared-data/
├── angular.json
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
└── node_modules/

The exact generated files depend on the Angular version and project configuration, but the overall structure is familiar.

Angular CLI provides commands for building, testing, serving, and generating code across these projects.

For example:

ng serve admin

ng build customer

ng test admin

We can also build libraries:

ng build shared-ui

For many workspaces, this is already enough.

Sharing a component

Let's create a reusable vehicle card.

// projects/shared-ui/src/lib/vehicle-card/vehicle-card.component.ts

import { Component, input } from '@angular/core';

export interface Vehicle {
  id: string;
  registration: string;
  model: string;
}

@Component({
  selector: 'shared-vehicle-card',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <article>
      <h3>{{ vehicle().registration }}</h3>
      <p>{{ vehicle().model }}</p>
    </article>
  `,
})
export class VehicleCardComponent {
  vehicle = input.required<Vehicle>();
}

We can export it from the library's public API:

// projects/shared-ui/src/public-api.ts

export * from './lib/vehicle-card/vehicle-card.component';

Then the admin application can import it:

import { Component } from '@angular/core';

import { VehicleCardComponent } from 'shared-ui';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-vehicle-list',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [VehicleCardComponent],
  template: `
    @for (vehicle of vehicles; track vehicle.id) {
      <shared-vehicle-card [vehicle]="vehicle" />
    }
  `,
})
export class VehicleListComponent {
  vehicles: Vehicle[] = [];
}

The customer application can use the same library.

This is a legitimate monorepo setup.

And we haven't needed Nx yet.

If your main requirement is simply sharing Angular libraries between a few applications, Angular CLI might already solve your problem.

3. What Changes When We Introduce Nx?

Nx doesn't replace Angular.

It builds on the Angular ecosystem and adds capabilities for managing larger workspaces.

According to the official Nx comparison, Angular CLI already supports application generation, libraries, building, testing, and local development.

Nx adds capabilities such as:

  • First-class monorepo tooling.
  • Project dependency graphs.
  • Enforced module boundaries.
  • Affected task execution.
  • Task orchestration.
  • Local task caching.
  • Remote caching.
  • Distributed task execution.

These are the differences worth exploring.

Creating an Nx workspace

We can create a new Angular workspace with Nx:

npx create-nx-workspace@latest company-platform \
  --template=nrwl/angular-template

The Angular template is available through Nx's workspace creation workflow.

Alternatively, we can migrate an existing Angular CLI workspace incrementally.

From the existing workspace:

npx nx add @nx/angular

This installs the Angular plugin and configures Nx integration.

It's important to keep Nx package versions compatible with each other. Using nx add is the recommended way to install the plugin into an existing Nx workspace.

Documentation:

  • Nx with Angular
  • Adding Nx to an existing workspace

Generating applications and libraries

With Nx, we can generate applications:

nx generate @nx/angular:app apps/admin

nx generate @nx/angular:app apps/customer

And libraries:

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/shared-ui

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/shared-data

Nx also supports more specific libraries:

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/vehicles/feature-list

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/vehicles/data-access

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/vehicles/ui

The exact generator options depend on the Nx and Angular versions, so check the Angular generator reference when building a real workspace.

A possible structure:

company-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── admin/
│   └── customer/
│
├── libs/
│   ├── shared/
│   │   ├── ui/
│   │   └── data-access/
│   │
│   └── vehicles/
│       ├── feature-list/
│       ├── data-access/
│       └── ui/
│
├── nx.json
├── package.json
└── tsconfig.base.json

This organization makes it easier to understand which libraries belong to which domain.

However, the folder structure alone isn't the most important difference.

The real value starts when Nx understands the relationships between projects.

4. Project Graph: Understanding Dependencies

Imagine our workspace has these projects:

admin
customer
shared-ui
vehicles-data-access
billing
reports

The applications depend on shared libraries:

admin
 ├── shared-ui
 └── vehicles-data-access

customer
 ├── shared-ui
 └── vehicles-data-access

As the workspace grows, these relationships become increasingly important.

A change to shared-ui might affect both applications.

A change to billing might affect only the administrative application.

Without a clear understanding of these dependencies, it's easy to lose track of what needs to be tested or rebuilt.

Nx builds a project graph that represents relationships between projects.

You can inspect it with:

nx graph

The interactive graph helps developers understand how applications and libraries depend on each other.

This becomes especially useful when a workspace contains dozens or hundreds of projects.

Angular CLI can manage multiple projects, but it doesn't provide the same first-class project graph visualization and dependency-aware workflow as Nx.

The distinction isn't that Angular CLI cannot organize projects.

It's that Nx makes relationships between projects a central part of the development workflow.

5. Enforcing Architectural Boundaries

This is one of the most interesting features of Nx.

Let's say we have two applications:

apps/
├── admin/
└── customer/

And some shared libraries:

libs/
├── shared/
│   ├── ui/
│   └── utils/
│
└── vehicles/
    ├── feature-list/
    └── data-access/

A reasonable dependency structure might be:

admin → vehicles/feature-list
admin → shared/ui

customer → vehicles/feature-list
customer → shared/ui

vehicles/feature-list → vehicles/data-access

vehicles/data-access → shared/utils

But what happens when someone starts importing application-specific code into a shared library?

For example:

// libs/shared/ui/src/lib/admin-widget.ts

import { AdminService } from
  '../../../../apps/admin/src/app/services/admin.service';

This is a serious architectural problem.

A shared library should not depend on a specific application.

The problem isn't merely that the import path is ugly.

The dependency direction is wrong.

The shared library now depends on an application that depends on the shared library.

This can create circular dependencies, difficult refactoring, and unpredictable build relationships.

Nx module boundary rules

Nx provides the @nx/enforce-module-boundaries ESLint rule.

We can use project tags to describe architectural roles.

For example:

{
  "name": "admin",
  "tags": ["scope:admin", "type:app"]
}

A shared UI library:

{
  "name": "shared-ui",
  "tags": ["scope:shared", "type:ui"]
}

A vehicles data-access library:

{
  "name": "vehicles-data-access",
  "tags": ["scope:vehicles", "type:data-access"]
}

We can then define dependency constraints in ESLint.

A simplified configuration might look like this:

// eslint.config.mjs

import nx from '@nx/eslint-plugin';

export default [
  {
    files: ['**/*.ts'],
    rules: {
      '@nx/enforce-module-boundaries': [
        'error',
        {
          depConstraints: [
            {
              sourceTag: 'type:app',
              onlyDependOnLibsWithTags: [
                'type:app',
                'type:feature',
                'type:ui',
                'type:data-access',
                'type:util',
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  },
];

This is an illustrative rule. A real workspace should define its constraints according to its architecture, and the exact ESLint configuration may vary with the Nx version and generated setup.

The important point is that Nx can help enforce architectural decisions instead of relying exclusively on code review.

This is a concrete benefit: Nx can help prevent certain dependency relationships from being introduced in the first place.

Angular CLI doesn't provide an equivalent first-class module-boundary enforcement feature.

6. The Performance Question: Is Nx Actually Faster?

This is where I think we need to be careful.

It's easy to find claims that Nx makes builds dramatically faster.

But performance depends on many factors:

  • Number of projects.
  • Number of dependencies.
  • Build configuration.
  • Test configuration.
  • Hardware.
  • CI environment.
  • Cache availability.
  • How much of the workspace changes.

A small Angular application might not see a meaningful improvement.

A large monorepo with many independent projects could benefit significantly.

Let's break down the relevant features.

6.1 Angular CLI already has caching

Before comparing Nx, we need to acknowledge something important.

Angular CLI already supports persistent disk caching.

For example:

ng build admin

Running the same build again can reuse cached work.

The cache is enabled by default for local development environments.

You can inspect its configuration:

ng cache info

And control it through the workspace configuration.

For example:

ng config cli.cache.environment all

Angular CLI cache documentation:

https://angular.dev/cli/cache

Therefore, it would be misleading to compare:

  • Angular CLI with caching disabled.
  • Nx with caching enabled.

That wouldn't be a fair comparison.

6.2 Nx adds task-level caching

Nx introduces caching at the task level.

A task might be:

nx build admin

Nx calculates a hash based on relevant inputs, including source files, dependencies, configuration, and other task inputs.

If the same task with the same relevant inputs has already completed, Nx can restore its cached outputs instead of executing the task again.

For example:

nx build admin

Run it again:

nx build admin

If the task is cacheable and its inputs haven't changed, Nx can restore the previous result.

This isn't simply caching Angular's compilation.

Nx can cache the results of different kinds of tasks, including builds, tests, linting, and other configured commands.

Documentation:

https://nx.dev/docs/features/cache-task-results

6.3 Running only affected projects

This is where Nx becomes particularly interesting.

Imagine a workspace with:

admin
customer
shared-ui
vehicles-data-access
billing
reports

A change to vehicles-data-access might affect:

vehicles-data-access
admin
customer

But it shouldn't necessarily require rebuilding:

billing
reports

Nx can determine which projects are affected by a change.

For example:

nx affected -t build

And:

nx affected -t test

These commands run the relevant tasks for affected projects.

This is particularly useful in CI, where running every build and test on every commit can become expensive.

The actual benefit depends on the dependency graph.

If every application depends on the same library, changing that library may affect nearly the entire workspace.

In that case, the number of skipped tasks will be smaller.

6.4 Parallel task execution

Nx can also run independent tasks in parallel.

For example:

nx run-many -t build

This runs build tasks across projects.

Nx's task graph determines which tasks can run concurrently and which depend on other tasks.

This can reduce total execution time when the workspace contains independent projects.

However, parallel execution also depends on available CPU and memory resources.

Running too many builds simultaneously can increase memory pressure and make the machine slower.

Parallelism is not automatically a performance improvement in every environment.

7. Remote Caching: A Different Kind of Benefit

Local caching is useful for individual developers.

Remote caching becomes particularly interesting for teams.

Imagine five developers working on the same workspace.

Developer A builds and tests a shared library.

Developer B later makes a change to an application that uses that library.

If the library's task inputs haven't changed, the previous result may be reusable.

Nx Cloud can share cache results between developers and CI environments.

This means the same task doesn't necessarily need to run repeatedly on every machine.

The workflow can look like this:

Developer A
    |
    | Build shared library
    v
Remote Cache
    |
    | Reuse result
    v
Developer B / CI

Nx Cloud documentation:

https://nx.dev/docs/features/ci-features/remote-cache

This can be valuable when:

  • Builds are expensive.
  • Many developers share the same workspace.
  • CI repeatedly executes similar tasks.
  • Projects have stable dependencies.

But remote caching introduces additional considerations:

  • Configuration.
  • Cache access and permissions.
  • Infrastructure or subscription costs, depending on the setup.
  • Correct task input and output configuration.

A cache is only useful when the system can safely determine that the previous result is valid.

8. Angular CLI vs Nx: A Practical Comparison

Let's summarize what we've discussed.

Capability Angular CLI Nx
Multiple Angular projects Yes Yes
Angular applications Yes Yes
Angular libraries Yes Yes
Shared components Yes Yes
Build, test, serve Yes Yes
Project dependency graph Limited compared with Nx First-class
Enforced module boundaries No equivalent built-in feature Yes
Affected project execution No equivalent first-class workflow Yes
Task-level caching Angular build cache Nx task cache
Remote caching Not built in Available through Nx Cloud
Distributed task execution Not built in Available through Nx Cloud
Additional tooling complexity Lower Higher

One detail matters here: Angular CLI and Nx are not mutually exclusive.

Nx integrates with Angular CLI builders and schematics.

You can continue using familiar Angular tooling while gradually introducing Nx features.

The official Nx comparison provides a more detailed overview.

9. Performance Benchmarks: Let's Measure Instead of Guessing

I think this is an important section to include in any serious comparison.

Rather than claiming that Nx is a certain percentage faster, we can create a reproducible benchmark.

Benchmark environment

Use a workspace with:

  • Two Angular applications.
  • Five shared libraries.
  • Unit tests for each application and library.
  • A production build configuration.
  • A fixed Node.js version.
  • A fixed Angular and Nx version.
  • The same machine and operating system.

Record the environment:

Operating System:
CPU:
RAM:
Node.js:
Package Manager:
Angular:
Nx:

Scenarios to measure

Scenario What we want to understand
Initial build Baseline execution time
Repeated build Cache effectiveness
Full workspace test Cost of running everything
Small application change Incremental build behavior
Shared library change Dependency impact
CI build Potential pipeline improvement
Remote cache hit Cross-machine reuse

Example benchmark commands

Angular CLI:

ng build admin
ng build customer

ng test admin
ng test customer

Nx:

nx build admin
nx build customer

nx test admin
nx test customer

Affected tasks:

nx affected -t build
nx affected -t test

For meaningful measurements, use the same workspace, equivalent build targets, and equivalent test coverage.

Important: Separate cold and warm runs

A cold run measures execution without reusable task results.

A warm run measures what happens when caches are available.

These are different scenarios and should not be mixed.

For each scenario:

  1. Run the task once.
  2. Record the initial execution.
  3. Run it again without changing inputs.
  4. Record the repeated execution.
  5. Repeat the experiment several times.
  6. Compare medians rather than relying on a single run.

For Nx, record whether the result came from:

  • Task execution.
  • Local cache.
  • Remote cache.

For Angular CLI, record the cache configuration and whether it was enabled.

Benchmark results template

Here is a table that could be included in the final article:

Scenario Angular CLI Nx Notes
Initial build TBD TBD Cold run
Repeated build TBD TBD Warm cache
Full test suite TBD TBD All projects
Small app change TBD TBD Incremental
Shared library change TBD TBD Affected projects
CI execution TBD TBD Pipeline comparison

I would only publish actual numbers after running the experiment.

If Nx is 20% faster in one scenario but only 3% faster in another, that's a much more interesting result than claiming it is universally faster.

It also makes the article more trustworthy.

10. When Does Nx Actually Make Sense?

Let's move away from features and focus on decisions.

Scenario 1: One Angular application 

my-app/
├── src/
├── angular.json
└── package.json

Nx probably isn't necessary.

Angular CLI provides everything required to develop, test, and build the application.

Introducing Nx might add concepts without solving a meaningful problem.

Scenario 2: Two independent applications 

company/
├── admin/
└── customer/

If these applications have:

  • Independent teams.
  • Independent releases.
  • Few shared dependencies.
  • Different lifecycles.

Separate repositories might be more appropriate.

A monorepo isn't automatically better simply because the applications belong to the same company.

Scenario 3: Multiple applications sharing a design system 

company-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── admin/
│   └── customer/
│
└── libs/
    └── shared-ui/

This is a reasonable monorepo candidate.

Angular CLI can support this structure.

Nx becomes more attractive if we need:

  • Architectural dependency rules.
  • Project graph visualization.
  • Selective builds and tests.
  • Better task orchestration.
  • Remote caching.

Scenario 4: A large workspace with many domains 

company-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── admin/
│   ├── customer/
│   └── operations/
│
└── libs/
    ├── vehicles/
    ├── appointments/
    ├── billing/
    ├── authentication/
    └── shared/

At this point, Nx can provide meaningful value.

The workspace needs more than a place to store projects.

It needs a way to understand dependencies, enforce architectural boundaries, and avoid unnecessary work.

Scenario 5: Microfrontends

Microfrontends introduce a different set of concerns.

Applications may share a repository but still need:

  • Independent deployment.
  • Independent ownership.
  • Runtime integration.
  • Separate release cycles.

A monorepo can support this arrangement, but it doesn't automatically solve microfrontend architecture.

Nx may help with workspace organization and CI, but deployment independence and runtime integration still require their own design.

11. A Practical Decision Checklist

Before adopting Nx, I would ask:

  • Do we have multiple applications or libraries that genuinely belong together?
  • Are dependencies between projects becoming difficult to understand?
  • Do we need architectural boundaries enforced automatically?
  • Are CI builds and tests executing unnecessary tasks?
  • Would task caching make a measurable difference?
  • Do we need to coordinate changes across applications?
  • Are the benefits worth introducing another tool into the development workflow?

If most answers are no, Angular CLI might be enough.

If several answers are yes, Nx deserves serious consideration.

The important part is not the number of applications.

It's the complexity of coordinating them.

12. My Take: Start Simple, Introduce Nx When the Problems Become Real

I don't think Nx should be the default answer to every Angular workspace.

Angular CLI is capable of managing multiple applications and libraries.

For smaller workspaces, that may be all you need.

But as a workspace grows, the problems change.

The challenge is no longer just creating applications or sharing components.

It becomes:

  • Understanding dependencies.
  • Enforcing architectural boundaries.
  • Avoiding unnecessary builds.
  • Coordinating tasks.
  • Improving CI performance.
  • Maintaining a consistent development workflow.

This is where Nx becomes valuable.

Not because it makes your architecture automatically better.

Not because every monorepo needs it.

But because it provides tooling for problems that become increasingly difficult to manage manually.

And that's the distinction I think matters most.

Don't introduce Nx because your project has multiple applications. Introduce it when the complexity of managing those applications becomes a problem that Nx can actually solve.

Final Thoughts

Monorepos are a strategy, not an architectural achievement.

Angular CLI already provides a solid foundation for organizing multiple applications and libraries.

Nx extends that foundation with project graphs, dependency constraints, task orchestration, caching, and CI optimization.

Those features can make a significant difference in larger workspaces.

But they also introduce additional concepts and configuration.

The best choice depends on the problems your team is facing today, not the scale you imagine your project might eventually reach.

I'd rather start with a simple workspace and introduce complexity when it becomes useful than build a sophisticated monorepo that solves problems we don't have.

What About Your Projects?

Have you adopted Nx in an Angular workspace?

Did it actually improve your development experience or CI performance?

Or did Angular CLI turn out to be enough?

I'm particularly interested in real-world experiences with affected builds, caching, and architectural boundaries.

articles.description: From a multi-agent testing experiment to a broader discussion about how engineering teams should...
articles.body_html:
From a multi-agent testing experiment to a broader discussion about how engineering teams should evolve in the age of AI.

At first, I simply wanted to share an AI-powered automated testing system I had been working on.

The system could already understand requirements, generate test cases, interact with web browsers and mobile apps, identify defects, and connect bug fixing with regression testing. I expected the session to focus on how AI could improve testing efficiency.

But during our internal session on November 5, 2026, the discussion gradually moved beyond testing.

We started talking about how product, development, and QA teams work together. We discussed why requirements so often fall out of sync, and how AI might change the way engineering teams are organized.

By the end of the discussion, the session had become the final push that helped set our company's organizational transformation in motion.

Looking back, I find that quite interesting. We set out to help testers work more efficiently with AI. Instead, we ended up discussing how AI might force the entire engineering organization to rethink the way it works.

1. 🤖 I Wanted AI to Handle the Entire Testing Process

I've been working on a multi-agent automated testing system.

Rather than simply asking AI to generate automation scripts from test cases, I wanted to connect the entire process: understanding requirements, designing tests, executing them, reporting defects, verifying fixes, and running regression tests.

The workflow looks roughly like this:

  1. AI reads product requirement documents and prototypes to understand business workflows and acceptance criteria.
  2. It generates test cases, which are then reviewed by multiple agents.
  3. Based on those test cases, AI controls web browsers and mobile apps, simulating real user interactions to execute the tests.
  4. When it finds an issue, AI generates a defect report and submits it to our issue-tracking system.
  5. Each reported defect goes through a second review and human confirmation before being assigned to the appropriate developer.
  6. After the developer fixes the issue, AI automatically runs regression tests to verify the fix and move the defect through the closure process, with human oversight retained.

The end-to-end workflow, from requirements to regression testing, is now in place and working.

What impressed me most was that AI had started taking over some of the most frustrating parts of traditional test automation.

With UI automation, the hardest part was often not writing the initial scripts. It was maintaining them.

A developer changes a UI component, and testers may have to revisit element locators, page objects, and interaction scripts. The more frequently the interface changes, the higher the maintenance cost. Sometimes, testers spend more time maintaining automation scripts than actually running tests.

Now, AI can observe the current page, understand its elements and interaction states, and perform actions based on the testing objectives. It still has to deal with UI changes and execution failures, but it can already take over a considerable amount of work that previously required repeated manual maintenance.

That made me reconsider the limits of automated testing.

2. 🔍 Automated Testing Should Do More Than Repeat Known Test Cases


For a long time, I held a fairly firm view of automated testing:

Automation is useful for regression testing, but it is not very good at discovering new defects.

The reason is straightforward. Traditional automated testing relies heavily on test cases designed in advance, fixed execution steps, and predefined assertions. It can repeatedly execute known test paths, but it struggles to discover problems that testers never thought to look for.

It behaves more like an executor that follows instructions than a tester capable of exploring software behavior.

But as AI agents emerged that could understand requirements, observe screens, analyze page states, and adapt their actions, I began to change my mind.

When training and refining the agents' testing behavior, I emphasized one principle:

Don't just follow the requirements document. And don't treat the test cases as the limits of your exploration.

Requirements describe what a product is expected to do, but they cannot cover every possible user behavior or system state.

So, after completing the tests defined by the requirements, AI should also explore additional scenarios, including:

  • Invalid and unexpected inputs: Empty values, excessively long text, illegal characters, unusual formats, and unexpected combinations of data.
  • Boundary conditions: Maximum and minimum values, threshold conditions, duplicate submissions, and unusual sequences of operations.
  • Abnormal workflows: Interrupted operations, repeated clicks, page refreshes, network failures, expired sessions, and inconsistent states between consecutive steps.
  • Security-related scenarios: Unauthorized access, permission boundaries, sensitive information exposure, and attempts to perform operations that should not be allowed.
  • Unexpected interactions: Skipping normal steps, performing rapid consecutive actions, repeatedly switching states, or accessing the same business function through different entry points.

Of course, this does not mean AI should be allowed to operate freely against production systems. The scope of exploration, test environments, account permissions, and operational risks must all be controlled. Security testing must also remain within clearly authorized boundaries.

I don't want AI to simply prove that the requirements have been implemented. I want it to look for problems that might emerge when the system is used in ways that were never anticipated.

This is where my understanding of automated testing has changed.

In the past, automation mainly repeated checks for known issues. Now, AI has the potential to help discover problems we didn't know to look for.

It cannot guarantee that every defect will be found, and it cannot replace human judgment. But automated testing no longer has to be limited to test cases written in advance.

3. 🌙 AI Works at Night. Humans Make the Decisions During the Day.


These days, I usually schedule automated testing tasks before finishing work.

The agents then continue running overnight. When I arrive at work the next morning, I can usually find a batch of defect reports already submitted by AI.

My job is to review those issues one by one, determine whether they are genuine and consistent with the current requirements, confirm them, and assign them to the appropriate developers.

This changes how testers spend their time.

Previously, testers had to spend a considerable amount of time operating systems, executing test cases, observing results, and preparing reports. Now, AI can take over a significant portion of that repetitive work, allowing people to focus more on evaluating issues, analyzing risks, and improving product quality.

However, this process also revealed another problem:

Finding a defect doesn't mean communicating it effectively.

Initially, AI-generated defect reports were often just dense blocks of text. They contained plenty of information, but they weren't particularly easy for developers to read.

If a report cannot help the person receiving it quickly understand the problem, then even a large amount of information does little to improve collaboration.

So I went through several rounds of adjustments to the reporting format. We needed more than a record of everything that happened during execution. The report had to clearly explain what happened, where the problem occurred, how the actual behavior differed from the expected behavior, and how the issue could be reproduced and verified.

After several iterations, the reports became much more readable and useful.

This made me realize that AI output quality should not be measured only by how much work it completes. We also need to consider whether the next person in the workflow can actually use the results.

After each testing cycle, I also ask AI to summarize the problems and lessons from that run. Experiences that have been reviewed, validated, and shown to be reusable are then distilled into general-purpose Skills.

That way, the next testing cycle doesn't have to start from scratch. It can build on what the previous cycle has learned.

In practice, this creates a continuous improvement loop:

Execute → Discover issues → Review → Capture lessons → Turn reusable knowledge into Skills → Start the next cycle.

4. 📊 The Numbers Show the Value, but Also Reveal Problems


In one of our knowledge-base projects, we've accumulated some concrete results:

Metric Result
Total defects identified 47
Defects identified by AI 36
Defects identified manually 11
Defects ultimately confirmed as valid 30
Valid defects contributed by AI 21

In other words, AI identified 21 of the 30 defects ultimately confirmed as valid, accounting for 70%.

These figures show that, within the scope of this project and its test coverage, AI is no longer just a tool for executing test cases. It is making a real contribution to defect discovery.

We've also experimented with having agents navigate pages, capture the API calls involved in business workflows, and run scheduled, full-scale API validation every day. Our current test environment covers nearly 300 APIs associated with business workflows.

These experiments show that AI can take on continuous testing tasks at both the UI and API levels.

But the data also reveals some problems.

For example, we currently have only one test environment. When multiple requirements are being developed in parallel, code changes can conflict, and deployments can interrupt other testing tasks. We still need to evaluate adding a second test environment and a dedicated performance testing environment.

Browser compatibility also needs further work, including test coverage for different Windows versions and the 360 browser.

These are infrastructure problems. They can be addressed gradually through additional resources and technical improvements.

What really made me think, however, was another category of problems.

5. 🧩 Automation Exposes Organizational Problems That Traditional Testing Often Hides


At one point, we noticed that some defects reported by AI were being classified as invalid.

Our first suspicion was naturally that AI might have misunderstood the requirements or that there was a problem with the testing logic.

But after looking more closely, we found that AI wasn't entirely to blame.

Some requirements had already been adjusted through discussions between product and development, but the official PRD had not been updated. Product and development might have reached a new understanding, or even made changes to the implementation privately, while QA and AI were still working from the original requirements document.

As a result, AI identified a discrepancy based on the official requirements, but the reported issue was considered invalid.

From a testing perspective, AI hadn't necessarily done anything wrong. From the development team's perspective, based on their current understanding of the implementation, the issue might not have been something they believed needed fixing.

The real problem was that the team was working with multiple versions of the same requirement context.

This led me to an important observation:

Automation can expose organizational problems that traditional manual testing has quietly absorbed and hidden for years.

In the past, testers often compensated for inconsistencies in requirements documents through verbal communication, ad hoc clarification, and their own experience. This work is important, but it can also make an organization believe that its processes are working perfectly well.

AI doesn't automatically know about a private conversation, nor can it understand the latest version of someone's thinking. It executes tasks based on the context it receives.

When the official documentation no longer matches the team's actual understanding, automation exposes that gap.

So the question isn't simply whether AI is smart enough.

We also need to ask: Does the team have a shared version of the requirements that everyone agrees on, that is kept up to date, and that AI can correctly interpret?

6. 🏢 Why Did a Technical Presentation Turn into a Discussion About Organizational Structure?


On November 5, 2026, we held an internal session to share our experience with local AI agents and automated testing. One of the company's founders also joined the discussion.

The original focus was AI testing capabilities, but the conversation gradually expanded to engineering workflows and organizational structure.

I increasingly agree with one observation:

AI is reducing the cost of producing code, but the cost of coordinating people isn't decreasing at the same pace.

In the past, a requirement might be analyzed and documented by a product manager, handed over to frontend and backend developers, and eventually passed to QA for verification. Every handoff meant that context had to be transferred again.

If any part of that chain involved a misunderstanding, rework could follow.

Now, AI can help product managers make certain code changes. It can help testers understand and modify code. It can also allow developers to participate more directly in requirement analysis and product design.

If a small requirement only needs a few code changes, but still has to pass through multiple roles, processes, and rounds of communication, the coordination cost may far exceed the actual coding cost.

This doesn't mean professional specialization has lost its value. Rather, AI is gradually lowering some of the capability barriers between traditional roles.

During our discussion, we proposed a direction: moving away from traditional role-based division of labor toward a more flexible model in which people can work across traditional role boundaries with the help of AI.

When we talk about a full-stack approach across the team, we don't mean that everyone must become a traditional full-stack engineer, or that people should abandon their professional expertise.

What we really mean is this:

People in product, development, and QA should all be able to use AI to cross their previous technical boundaries and help solve the problems they understand.

For example:

  • Product managers can use AI to make code changes and verify smaller requirements themselves.
  • Developers can participate in requirement analysis earlier and take overall ownership of larger initiatives.
  • Testers don't have to stop at submitting bug reports when they discover defects. They can use AI to investigate the issue and even modify code, with developers providing the necessary review and confirmation.

For small requirements, we want to reduce unnecessary handoffs. For larger initiatives, we want to assign a clear owner to coordinate the entire process.

This isn't about eliminating professional roles. It's about reducing the information loss caused by rigid boundaries between them.

7. 🔗 Collaboration Should Start with Requirements, Not After Testing Finds a Problem


To make this way of working possible, we first need to address the problem of shared requirement context.

We discussed several concrete directions.

First, product, development, and QA should participate in requirement alignment from the beginning, rather than waiting until the PRD is finished and development is complete before testers start trying to understand the requirements.

Second, we want to establish a standardized PRD Skill and structured templates so that requirement documents follow a more consistent format.

More importantly, whenever requirements change, the official documentation must be updated promptly. Changes should not exist only in private conversations between a few people.

We also discussed a more ambitious idea: using recordings from smart badges to identify requirement changes during discussions, flag content that might affect the requirements, and assist in updating the PRD. The proposed changes would then be submitted to the relevant people for review and approval.

This is still an idea to be explored, not a feature that has already been deployed.

But the underlying principle is clear:

We should make sure the team's actual shared understanding is captured promptly in a form that everyone can use.

Beyond PRDs, we also need shared development and testing Skills, coding standards, and Specs.

When product, development, and QA work from a reasonably consistent context, AI can become a tool that connects different parts of the workflow instead of creating more isolated information silos between roles.

8. 🚀 From Individual AI Tools to an AI-Driven Engineering System


The discussion eventually moved beyond any particular agent or automated testing tool.

We started looking at the engineering system as a whole.

For example:

  • Building shared Skill libraries for development and testing.
  • Standardizing coding conventions and Spec management.
  • Creating a complete workflow: retrieving defects from Yunxiao, using AI to fix them, running automated regression tests, and retaining human review.
  • Exploring automated effort estimation and requirement classification.
  • Continuing to improve test environments and browser compatibility.
  • Ensuring that requirement changes are communicated promptly to reduce unnecessary discussions and rework.

These initiatives won't be completed automatically after a single meeting. The organizational transformation plan has already been launched, and progress will be reviewed and coordinated through weekly updates.

Of course, having a clear direction and an initiated plan doesn't mean the road ahead will be smooth.

Once implementation begins, we'll inevitably encounter practical obstacles: the inertia of existing processes, established collaboration habits between different roles, limitations in technical infrastructure, and the challenges of fitting new ways of working into existing business rhythms.

These problems can't be solved through one meeting or a few new rules. We'll need to identify issues as they arise, adjust our approach, and gradually develop a working model that actually fits the team.

For me, this is what makes the discussion meaningful. It wasn't just about proposing an idea for organizational change. The plan has already moved into the implementation stage.

An AI-driven engineering system can't be built simply by purchasing a few tools, connecting some APIs, or creating a handful of agents.

It requires technical capabilities, process standards, accumulated knowledge, and organizational collaboration to evolve together.

If information within the team remains inconsistent, even the most capable AI will simply execute the wrong context more efficiently.

9. 💡 In the AI Era, Coding Ability May No Longer Be the Rarest Resource


Looking back, I initially just wanted AI to help me automate more testing work.

But as AI began to understand requirements, interact with interfaces, actively explore abnormal scenarios, submit defects, assist with fixes, and perform regression testing, I realized that I needed to rethink more than just testing. I needed to rethink the entire software development process.

In the past, many efficiency problems were attributed to a lack of capability in a particular role, or to a specific stage of the process not being fast enough.

Now, AI is making more and more tasks easier.

But as writing code becomes easier, what may actually slow down development is the failure to synchronize requirements, unclear ownership, and too many handoffs between people.

I don't believe AI will turn everyone into a programmer, nor do I think software teams will no longer need professional roles such as product, development, and QA.

I believe AI will gradually remove unnecessary barriers between these roles.

People who understand a problem should be able to use AI to move toward a solution more directly, rather than having to wait for information to pass through multiple roles.

For testers, this means going beyond executing test cases to participating in risk exploration, problem analysis, and quality improvement.

For developers, it means taking responsibility not just for receiving requirements and writing code, but for solving a more complete problem.

For product managers, it means going beyond describing requirements and using AI to validate and implement their ideas more directly.

Ultimately, a team's competitiveness may no longer depend on how many people complete how many separate tasks. It may depend on whether the team can move accurate information quickly and enable everyone to use AI to solve more complete problems.

An AI testing presentation eventually became a discussion about how the entire engineering organization should change.

Perhaps this is one of the most important changes to pay attention to in the AI era:

AI is making coding easier, but what will truly make software development faster may be our willingness to redesign the way people work together.

articles.title: Floating Versions Are an Open Door: Pin Your Actions and Dependencies
articles.description: The problem   Look at almost any CI workflow and you'll find a line like this:    - uses:...
articles.body_html:
The problem

Look at almost any CI workflow and you'll find a line like this:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4

Open almost any package.json and you'll see this:

"dependencies": { "some-sdk": "^0.5.0" }

And in a Python project, often just this:

litellm

All three say: give me whatever the latest acceptable version is right now. It feels responsible, since you get patches automatically. But it also means the code you run today is not the code you ran yesterday, and nobody reviewed the difference.

In 2026 that trade-off no longer works: the fastest way into thousands of companies is not to break their code, but to change the code they download.

Why "latest" is now a liability

The past few months have been a showcase of what floating versions cost.

On October 21, a compromised release of the popular LLM proxy LiteLLM was published to PyPI and Docker Hub. It was live for about two hours. Anyone who ran pip install litellm without a version, or whose auto-updater followed latest, got a credential stealer that ran on every Python start on the machine.

On October 8, version 0.5.144 of the Tensorlake npm SDK shipped a new variant of the Shai-Hulud worm. A dependency declared as ^0.5.0 would happily resolve to it. The worm stole tokens and republished the victim's other packages.

Earlier this year the same worm family hit TanStack: 84 malicious versions of 42 packages, all with valid provenance. A downstream project merged a routine Dependabot bump 24 minutes after it opened, and the worm used its token to publish 110 more.

GitHub Actions has the same weakness, in a sneakier form. A tag like @v4 is not a version at all. It's a movable pointer that the action's maintainer, or anyone who steals their credentials, can retarget to a different commit at any time. That's exactly what happened in the 2025 tj-actions/changed-files incident (CVE-2025-30066): attackers moved existing version tags to a malicious commit, and every workflow that referenced those tags started dumping its CI secrets into public build logs.

The pattern is always the same. Pinning doesn't make malicious code safe, but floating versions let malicious code reach you automatically, immediately and silently.

Why an exact version isn't enough: pin by SHA

The usual advice is "pin exact versions". It's a good start, but it isn't enough, because a version number is just a name, and names can be moved.

A Git tag like v4.2.2 is exactly as movable as v4: whoever controls the repository can point it at a different commit. Docker tags are mutable too, even precise ones. In the LiteLLM incident, the real v1.107.0 tag pointed at the attacker's image. On PyPI, maintainers can add new files to a release that already exists. And none of this matters if your manifest still accepts the next version that a hijacked account publishes.

The only identifier that can't be reassigned is a cryptographic hash of the content: a commit SHA, an image digest, a package integrity hash. Change one byte and the hash changes, so the install fails loudly instead of succeeding silently. That's the real meaning of pinning, and it has three parts.

1. Pin by hash, not by name. Your manifest can express intent (^4.2.0), but what you install must come from a lockfile that records, for every package (direct and transitive), the exact version and its integrity hash. For Actions and containers, the reference itself should be the SHA or digest. Commit the lockfile and install from it, never around it.

2. Enforce the hash at install time. A hash in a file is useless if nothing checks it. Use the installer modes that verify every artifact against the lockfile and refuse anything that doesn't match: npm ci, pip install --require-hashes, uv sync --locked, cargo build --locked.

3. Update deliberately, with a delay. Pinning is not "never update". Replace silent drift with automated update pull requests that wait a few days before proposing a new release. Most malicious versions are pulled within hours, so a short cooldown filters out the bulk of them.

The fix, ecosystem by ecosystem

GitHub Actions. Reference actions by full 40-character commit SHA, not by tag. That includes exact tags like @v4.2.2, which can be retargeted just like @v4. Keep the human-readable tag as a comment:

- uses: actions/checkout@<full-40-character-commit-sha> # v4.2.2

Dependabot and Renovate bump the SHA and the comment together. Even better, workflow lockfiles are now generally available on every GitHub plan: gh actions-lock writes .github/workflows/actions.lock with the exact commit of every action, transitive ones included, and admins can enforce it with the Require lockfile policy.

npm (and pnpm, Yarn). Commit package-lock.json (or pnpm-lock.yaml / yarn.lock) and use npm ci in CI, never npm install. npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says and verifies every sha512 integrity hash. Add ignore-scripts=true to .npmrc, since install-time scripts are how Shai-Hulud runs, and allow-list the few packages that need them.

Python. Unpinned requirements.txt files are why LiteLLM spread so fast. Use a real lockfile: uv lock with uv sync --locked, poetry.lock, or pip-tools with pip-compile --generate-hashes, then install with pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt. pip then refuses any file whose hash doesn't match, even under the same version number.

Containers. latest is the ^ of Docker, and even :1.107.0 is only a tag. Pin images by digest:

FROM python:3.13-slim@sha256:<digest>

And don't let auto-updaters pull production images straight from a public registry. Let a bot propose the new digest in a pull request instead.

Everything else. Commit Cargo.lock and build with --locked, rely on go.sum and the Go checksum database, and commit Gemfile.lock or composer.lock. Every mature ecosystem already has a hash-carrying lockfile; the work is to enforce it in CI.

A Monday checklist

  1. Commit a lockfile with integrity hashes in every repository, and make CI fail when it's missing or stale.
  2. Switch CI installs to hash-verifying modes: npm ci, uv sync --locked, pip install --require-hashes and cargo build --locked.
  3. Pin every GitHub Action by full commit SHA (a version tag is not enough).
  4. Pin container images by @sha256 digest, never by tag, and turn off blind auto-updates in production.

Conclusion

Floating versions turn every upstream compromise into your compromise, automatically, and even exact version names can be moved. Pin by SHA and hash, enforce them at install time. You'll still get every security patch, just a few days later and with your eyes open.

You can follow me on GitHub, where I'm creating cool projects.

I hope you enjoyed this article, until next time 👋

Giorgio Boa

Giorgio Boa is a full stack developer and the front-end ecosystem is his passion. He is also international public speaker, active in open source ecosystem, he loves learn and studies new things.

articles.title: Stop Swapping Models: Optimizing the Agent Environment Cuts 70% More Cost
articles.description: When an agent workflow runs up an unsustainable token bill, developers usually pull two levers.  The...
articles.body_html:
When an agent workflow runs up an unsustainable token bill, developers usually pull two levers.

The first lever is swapping the model. You take tasks running on a frontier model and try to force them onto an 8B open-weight model, or you spend weeks attempting to train a prompt router to predict which model can handle each step. The second lever is harness engineering. You rewrite system prompts, enforce structured outputs, add step-by-step reflection rules, and hope the agent stops making redundant tool calls.

Both levers hit diminishing returns quickly. Smaller models drop subtle context and fail multi-step tool sequences, while prompt engineering adds token overhead to every turn.

Almost nobody touches the environment.

We treat the workspace where the agent operates as an immutable surface. We point the agent at a chaotic directory of raw files, give it uncurated terminal access, expose raw OpenAPI schemas with hundreds of parameters, and let it inspect database tables by querying raw catalogs. The agent burns through context windows attempting to orient itself before it writes a single line of useful code.

A paper from researchers at UC Berkeley and UT Austin demonstrates why this default is backward. Titled "EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments" (arXiv:2611.07372, by Mingxuan Li, Huanzhi Mao, Qiuyang Mang, Hanchen Li, Joseph E. Gonzalez, and Alex Dimakis), the study shows that optimizing the stationary environment cuts token costs far more effectively than model swaps or prompt tweaks, without degrading task success.

Stationary environments in production

The paper focuses on what the authors call stationary environments.

In production deployments, agents rarely run in sterile single-turn sandboxes. They operate inside persistent environments shared across hundreds or thousands of tasks. A coding agent repeatedly navigates the same monolithic git repository. A support assistant searches the same corporate Slack workspace and ticketing platform. A data pipeline agent queries the same warehouse schemas.

The underlying artifacts in these environments stay relatively static, yet agents interact with them through raw, unoptimized interfaces.

To measure the impact of restructuring these spaces, the researchers built EnvOpt, a framework that uses an automated research agent to re-architect the environment representation for a given set of tasks. The optimizer restructures stored data, builds helper programs, generates local cheatsheets, and refines tool interfaces, testing changes against task performance without requiring human-labeled reference answers.

The resulting numbers on standard benchmarks challenge the standard playbook for reducing agent costs.

On AutomationBench, optimizing the stationary environment reduced the token cost of Claude Haiku 4.5 by 72.7 percent while raising its pass rate by 14.34 percent.

The optimization also transferred across model families. Deploying the same optimized environment to Claude Opus 5 reduced its operational cost by 68.1 percent with a 1.34 percent accuracy improvement.

When combined with harness optimization, the gains compounded. Stacking the optimized environment on top of Meta-Harness lowered Haiku 4.5 costs by a further 83.4 percent and added 11.17 percent accuracy over Meta-Harness alone. On Data-Eng-Bench, which evaluates agents on complex dbt data engineering tasks, the optimized environment reduced token expenses by 53.44 percent with zero loss in pass rate.

Where the token bill actually comes from

The authors tracked token consumption across input categories, output categories, tool calls, and environment feedback to pinpoint where the savings originated.

The results showed that the bulk of wasted spend does not come from model reasoning or final output generation. The largest token sink sits in environment feedback: the massive blocks of raw text, bloated JSON objects, and verbose error traces returned by exploratory tool calls.

When an agent needs to locate a ticket ID, find a function signature, or verify a schema, it issues exploratory queries. If the environment returns raw, unstructured dumps, the agent's context window inflates instantly. In subsequent turns, the model carries that accumulated noise forward, multiplying costs on every step.

The environment optimizations that produced the largest cost reductions shared a common pattern: they eliminated exploratory loops before the agent triggered them.

The most effective patterns were practical and straightforward:

  1. Pre-parsing messy payloads. On workspace automation tasks, helper scripts converted raw spreadsheets and multi-part emails into clean, plain-text summary blocks containing only the sender, subject, message ID, and relevant body chunks. The agent read clean text directly instead of burning tokens on repeated file-parsing tool invocations.

  2. Static API cheatsheets. Instead of requiring the agent to call discovery tools like api_search or api_fetch to understand endpoint parameters, the optimizer generated local text reference sheets for common Jira, Slack, and accounting actions. Having exact command structures available eliminated multi-turn trial calls.

  3. Filesystem index maps. In large file trees simulating enterprise workspaces, the optimizer compiled a single flat index file listing file paths, sizes, and file categories. The target agent could run a single grep command against the index instead of recursing through directories with find or ls.

  4. Local SQLite metadata caches. On data engineering benchmarks, the optimizer built an SQLite database indexing table definitions, upstream dependencies, and write destinations. Rather than reading dozens of dbt SQL models to trace lineage, the agent ran a single targeted SQL query.

The optimizations that failed

The paper also documents environment optimizations that failed during evaluation, and these failures offer useful warnings for production builders.

The first failure mode was the mega-file trap. In data engineering tasks, the research agent attempted to build a comprehensive reference file listing every possible value for every column across the database. The intention was to give the agent complete context in one place.

Instead, the massive file encouraged the target agent to make additional tool calls. Seeing a huge catalog of potential values caused the model to launch speculative exploration runs, ultimately increasing total token spend.

The second failure mode was imprecise search helpers. The optimizer built a custom search tool to help agents locate workspace documents. While the tool successfully identified relevant files, its ranking was too broad and included several adjacent files. Seeing those extra matches prompted the agent to read each one, driving up token consumption and execution time.

The third failure mode was rigid verification scripts. In repository debugging tasks, the optimizer introduced validation checks that rejected specific code patterns. While this saved time on early training tasks, it caused the agent to reject valid alternative patches on unseen problems, forcing it into costly recovery loops.

Engineering the workspace

The takeaway for software engineers building production agent workflows is clear.

When an agent gets expensive or unreliable, jumping immediately to fine-tuning or prompt rewrites is often the wrong first step. Look at the workspace you hand the agent. If the model has to run four shell commands just to discover which files matter, or parse a 400-line JSON payload to find two IDs, the environment is leaking tokens.

Structuring the environment with plain-text indexes, lightweight local SQLite caches, and clean CLI cheatsheets gives smaller models the footing they need to succeed at a fraction of the operating cost.

articles.title: When an AI Agent Says 'Done,' What Exactly Has Finished?
articles.description: "Done." It's probably the most satisfying word in a coding-agent session.  It can also conceal three...
articles.body_html:
"Done." It's probably the most satisfying word in a coding-agent session.

It can also conceal three very different questions:

  1. Was the work permitted?
  2. Did the work actually happen?
  3. Did the result achieve what we needed?

All three matter. A single green checkmark can make them look like one decision.

A small scenario

Imagine asking a coding agent to update validation logic under src/**.

It edits the code, reports that its tests passed, and declares the task complete. Everything looks fine until you ask what the status actually proves.

  • The task was assigned to an implementer with a declared src/** write scope. But did the runtime enforce that scope for the tools the agent used?
  • The plan called for independent review. But who actually reviewed the final revision, and was that the revision ultimately merged?
  • The agent says the feature works. But was that checked in the environment where users experience it?

These are separate evidence problems. Passing a test suite answers something useful about the tested code. It cannot, by itself, answer the other two questions.

One failure you can reproduce without an AI model

I maintain Agent Role Contracts (ARC), an open-source checker for declared agent roles, scope, reviews, and handoffs.

Its quickstart uses a deliberately simple setup:

Declared rule Requested task Preflight result
Implementer may write within src/** Update src/example.mjs PASS
Same declared rule Update secrets/production.txt TASK_WRITE_SCOPE_OUTSIDE_AUTHORITY
Same declared rule Correct the request to src/example.mjs PASS

You can run the published source demo with Git, Node.js 22.5+, and npm:

git clone https://github.com/suirindo/agent-role-contracts.git
npm --prefix agent-role-contracts run demo --silent

The repository's documented sequence is PASS → expected FAIL → PASS. It reads fictional JSON declarations; it starts no agent and writes no target file. The intentional rejection demonstrates one narrow property: a requested scope conflicts with the declared authority.

That's useful precisely because the check has a clear boundary. A declaration PASS does not authenticate the executor, enforce filesystem permissions, verify an actual review, or authorize execution. The host system must supply those controls.

A completion report with three layers

For real work, I'd like completion reports to distinguish these layers:

Layer A useful receipt What remains to establish
Contract Current task, scope, responsible role, review route, and the check result Whether the declared actors and permissions are genuine
Execution Exact commit or artifact, command results, and observable side-effect receipts Whether anything unobserved or uncertain occurred
Acceptance Independent review of the exact candidate, acceptance tests, and production observation where relevant Whether the user-facing outcome meets the original request

That produces a much more useful sentence than "Done":

Implementation completed and local tests passed. Independent review is pending. Production behavior has not yet been checked.

It is less triumphant. It is much more actionable.

The uncomfortable question

As agents become more autonomous, the word complete is becoming a product-interface decision. If the interface compresses implementation, verification, and acceptance into one status, the human operator inherits the uncertainty later.

Some teams will reasonably keep these stages separate in CI, IAM, and their runtime. Others may want a small declaration check before dispatch. ARC handles that narrower declaration problem; the broader evidence chain belongs to the surrounding system.

For teams using coding agents today: what is the minimum evidence you require before an agent is allowed to say "done"?

Is a passing test suite enough for internal tasks? Do you require an independent reviewer, an exact artifact identifier, a live check, or different thresholds depending on the side effect?

I'd be particularly interested in answers from teams that have already found a simpler solution.

Disclosure: I maintain Agent Role Contracts at Netsujo. The example above is a synthetic declaration check, not a production incident. Read the quickstart and limitations.

articles.body_html:
A few weeks ago I wrote about how I stopped coding and started orchestrating. Ten terminal tabs, three startups, me pressing Enter all day. Then I moved the whole setup to a Mac mini, put an orchestrator agent in charge of a pool of workers (coding agents, a design agent, a DevOps agent, an accounting agent), and went from 1 PR a day to 22.

I called myself an orchestrator. Then a manager of orchestrators. Both titles felt a bit grand for what I was actually doing.

With my daughter a couple of weeks away, I started re-reading my favorite book of Adler psychology, the courage to be happy. One idea stuck: the job of a parent is not to do things for the child, or to tell the child what to do all day. The job is to educate the child so that one day they can fend for themselves.

I read that sentence with my phone on my knee and the orchestrator asking me for the third time that morning whether it could run a migration.

And it clicked. I had the wrong job title all along.

You are not a product manager. You are an educator.

The industry has settled on two words for what humans do with AI agents: product manager and orchestrator. I think both are wrong, and the wrong word leads to the wrong setup.

A product manager writes a ticket, hands it over, and waits for the result. That is how I used my first workers. Every task started from zero. The agent didn't know my codebase conventions, didn't know we deploy with Kamal, and didn't know I hate service objects with more than one public method. So I wrote it all in the ticket. Every. Single. Time.

An orchestrator is worse. An orchestrator decides every move. That is the setup that turned me into a finger pressing Enter. The agents had no autonomy because I had given them none. I was not slow because the AI was slow; I was slow because I was the bottleneck in every decision.

An educator does something different. Adler is careful with the word: a teacher transmits facts; an educator shapes a person who can live on their own. An educator spends time up front so that later the child does not need them. You explain how the world works, you let them try, you correct, and you step back a bit more each time. The goal of the educator is to become unnecessary.

That is exactly what happened with my orchestrator without me noticing. It did not become useful because I gave it better tickets. It became useful because it knows how I work, what security I need, which decisions it can take alone and which ones to escalate to me. I educated it, mostly by accident.

Once I saw it as education, I started doing it on purpose.

Human knowledge, and AI knowledge

Adler makes a distinction I found useful. There is the knowledge you learn at school (maths, history, how to read), and there is a second kind of knowledge nobody writes an exam about: the shared rules for living with other people. You stop at a red light. You don’t talk in the cinema. You bring something when you are invited to dinner. Nobody is born with this. Every generation learns it from the previous one, and a child who does not learn it cannot function in society no matter how smart they are.

AI agents are in exactly that situation. The model is the smartest kid in the class. It knows Rails better than I do, it has read more Postgres documentation than any human alive. What it does not know is how to live in my house.

I started calling this AI knowledge: the basic set of rules an agent needs to perform tasks and fulfill its goals inside a specific environment. Not model weights, not prompts. The equivalent of knowing where the traffic lights are.

For my setup, AI knowledge looks like this:

Where things live: which repo is which startup, where the Obsidian vault is, which folder is the accounting drive.

How we ship: branch naming, PR size, what a green pipeline means, that nothing deploys on Friday evening Bali time.

What is dangerous: which commands need a human, which tables you never touch in production, what counts as a customer-facing change.

Who does what: the orchestrator dispatches, coding workers write and test, the design agent owns the UI, the DevOps agent deploys and monitors, the accounting agent does the books, I do strategy and the final say on money.

What already happened: decisions from co-founder meetings, bugs we already fixed last year, features we tried and killed.

None of this is in the model. All of it is in markdown files, a vault, and a handful of CLAUDE.md files that I keep adding to every time an agent does something that makes me say “no, not like that”.

The test is simple. If a brand new worker spins up tomorrow, can it fend for itself in my codebase with zero instructions from me? If the answer is no, I have not finished educating it. I have just written a very long ticket.

Knowledge only survives if it gets passed on

Human knowledge persists for one reason: people pass it forward. My parents taught me, I will teach my daughter; she will teach hers. Nobody re-derives the rules of society from scratch every morning.

Agents, by default, do exactly that. Every session starts from zero. Every worker is a newborn. Whatever a worker learned yesterday (that the test suite is flaky on the mailer specs, that the staging database has a weird extension) dies with its context window.

So the second part of the educator’s job is to make sure the knowledge outlives the one who learned it.

In practice, this means agents educating agents. Here is how it works in my setup:

A worker finishes a task and writes what it learned into the vault: a gotcha, a decision, a convention it discovered by breaking something.

The orchestrator reviews it. If it is a real rule and not a one-off, it goes into the shared AI knowledge. If it is noise, it gets dropped.

The next worker that touches that area reads it before starting.

I am not in that loop. That is the point. If I were the only channel through which knowledge moves between agents, I would be back to being the bottleneck, just with a nicer job title.

The nice side effect: when the orchestrator stops me from building a feature we already tried and killed last year, that is not the orchestrator being smart. That is a worker from eight months ago educating a worker from today, with me doing nothing.

What a well-educated agent looks like

Adler says a well-educated child has two things: they can take care of themselves, and they can live in harmony with others. I have found no better definition of a good agent.

1. Self-reliance

The agent can get from a task to a merged PR inside my environment without asking me anything. It knows where to look, how to run the tests, how to deploy, when to stop. The number I track for this is interruptions per task. When I started, it was 10 to 15 “allow this command?” per worker. Today the orchestrator absorbs almost all of them and escalates maybe one real decision a day to me.

This is also the one that lets me close the laptop. An agent that cannot fend for itself needs a human at the keyboard. An agent that can needs a Mac mini and a UPS.

2. Harmony with the environment

This is the one most people skip, and it is where agents do the most damage. A self-reliant agent with no sense of the environment is a toddler with a credit card. Very capable, very fast, zero awareness of what is around it.

Harmony means three things in my setup:

  1. Not recreating what already exists. The worker checks the vault and the codebase before writing a new service, a new helper, a new landing page section. The number of duplicated utility classes I had before this rule was embarrassing.

  2. Calling the right tool when needed. If there is a connector for Gmail, use it. If there is a script that generates invoices, run it, do not re-implement it in Ruby from scratch because you can. The right tool includes other agents: a coding worker that hits an accounting question hands it to the accounting agent; it does not improvise Singapore tax law. A worker that needs a new screen asks the design agent, it does not invent its own button style.

  3. Operating in sync with everyone else. Workers run in parallel. Thirty of them on a good night. One worker rewriting the User model while another one is adding a column to it is the agent version of two kids fighting over the same toy. The orchestrator’s job is to sequence them, and each worker’s job is to check what is in flight before it starts.

Self-reliance without harmony gives you fast chaos. Harmony without self-reliance gives you a polite agent that asks permission for everything. You need both, and you only get both by educating the agent, not by writing better tickets.

In Summary

If you take one thing from this post: stop asking “how do I write a better prompt” and start asking “what does this agent need to know to live here without me”.

Your role with AI is not product manager and not orchestrator. It is an educator, in Adler’s sense: someone whose job is to become unnecessary.

AI knowledge is the set of shared rules an agent needs to fend for itself in your environment. It lives in your repo and your vault, not in the model.

Knowledge persists better if agents pass it to other agents instead of simple .md files. If you are the only channel, you are the bottleneck.

A well-educated agent is self-reliant and in harmony with its environment. It does not rebuild what exists; it calls the right tool, and it stays in sync with the other agents.

Now, let’s educate.

Dani,
