articles.title: I Stamped Every Row With DateTime.Now and Paid Twice
articles.description: DateTime.Now is DateTime.UtcNow plus a trip through your local time zone rules, and that trip isn't free in a hot loop. I counted: on a box with a real time zone it roughly doubles the cost of reading the clock.
articles.body_html:
I had a batch importer stamping DateTime.Now onto every row it processed. A few hundred thousand rows, one timestamp each, nothing I'd ever think twice about. Then I put a profiler on the thing because it was slower than it had any right to be, and there it was near the top: reading the clock. Not the database, not the parsing. The clock.

So I did the thing I always end up doing. I counted.

Now is UtcNow wearing a coat

DateTime.Now doesn't read a "local clock." There's no such thing. It reads UTC, exactly like DateTime.UtcNow does, and then converts that instant into local time using TimeZoneInfo.Local. That conversion is the whole difference between the two calls. One reads the clock. The other reads the clock and then asks the time zone database what your offset is right now, DST and all.

The offset lookup is the part that costs. And here's the bit that surprised me: it costs even when the answer is zero.

Putting a clock on the clock

I read each one 20 million times, summed the ticks so nothing got optimized away, best of five rounds. Same loop, three bodies.

static long ReadUtcNow() => DateTime.UtcNow.Ticks;
static long ReadNow()    => DateTime.Now.Ticks;
static long ReadStopwatch() => Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

First run, on the container as it ships, which pins itself to UTC:

Local time zone: Etc/UTC

20,000,000 reads, best of 5
  DateTime.UtcNow     661.5 ms     33.1 ns/call
  DateTime.Now        911.8 ms     45.6 ns/call
  Now / UtcNow         1.38x

A UTC box has a zero offset. There's nothing to add. And Now is still almost 40% slower, because it does the lookup to find out the offset is zero. The work happens whether or not it changes the answer.

Then I pointed TZ at a real zone, the kind your laptop or an on-prem server actually runs, with daylight saving rules to evaluate:

Local time zone: America/New_York

20,000,000 reads, best of 5
  DateTime.UtcNow     678.3 ms     33.9 ns/call
  DateTime.Now      1,357.2 ms     67.9 ns/call
  Now / UtcNow         2.00x

Twice the cost. UtcNow sits around 33 ns no matter what I do; Now lands somewhere between 60 and 68 ns across runs. The time zone isn't part of reading the clock. It's a question Now asks afterward, every single time.

This is a container, not a lab, so I care about the ratio, not the exact nanoseconds. The ratio was steady run to run. Roughly double on a real zone, roughly a third extra on UTC.

The tool I actually wanted

Half the time I reach for DateTime.Now I'm not even recording a wall-clock time. I'm measuring how long something took. For that, both Now and UtcNow are the wrong tool, because they drag calendar math into a job that's really just "count ticks between here and there." Stopwatch does exactly that and nothing else:

  Stopwatch.GetTimestamp   637.3 ms     31.9 ns/call

Cheapest of the three, and it never touches a time zone or even cares what day it is. If you're timing a block of code, this is the one.

When I'd leave it alone

If you call DateTime.Now a handful of times per request, this whole post is noise. Thirty-odd extra nanoseconds disappears against literally anything else your code does. I'm not going to rewrite a login handler to shave that off, and neither should you. The importer only cared because it was reading the clock once per row, hundreds of thousands of times, in a loop that otherwise did very little. Hot path, high count. That's the only place it shows up.

And don't go blindly swapping Now for UtcNow in display code. If you're formatting a timestamp a human is going to read, they want their local time, and UtcNow will happily show them the wrong hour. That's a correctness bug, and no benchmark makes it worth shipping.

My own rule, for what it's worth: compute and store in UTC, read the clock with UtcNow, time things with Stopwatch, and convert to local exactly once, at the edge, right before a person sees it. Local time is a presentation concern. Treating it like a data concern is how you end up paying the time zone tax a few hundred thousand times to import a file nobody's even looking at yet.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself. New console project targeting net10.0, drop this in Program.cs, then dotnet run -c Release, and TZ="America/New_York" dotnet run -c Release for the wider gap:

using System.Diagnostics;

Console.WriteLine($"Local time zone: {TimeZoneInfo.Local.Id}");

const int Iterations = 20_000_000;
const int Rounds = 5;

// Warm up both paths so the JIT and the time-zone cache are hot.
_ = Measure(ReadUtcNow, 1_000_000);
_ = Measure(ReadNow, 1_000_000);

long utcTicks = long.MaxValue, nowTicks = long.MaxValue, swTicks = long.MaxValue;
for (int r = 0; r < Rounds; r++)
{
    utcTicks = Math.Min(utcTicks, Measure(ReadUtcNow, Iterations));
    nowTicks = Math.Min(nowTicks, Measure(ReadNow, Iterations));
    swTicks  = Math.Min(swTicks,  Measure(ReadStopwatch, Iterations));
}

double utcMs = utcTicks * 1000.0 / Stopwatch.Frequency;
double nowMs = nowTicks * 1000.0 / Stopwatch.Frequency;
double swMs  = swTicks  * 1000.0 / Stopwatch.Frequency;

Console.WriteLine($"{Iterations:N0} reads, best of {Rounds}");
Console.WriteLine($"  DateTime.UtcNow        {utcMs,8:N1} ms   {utcMs * 1e6 / Iterations,5:N1} ns/call");
Console.WriteLine($"  DateTime.Now           {nowMs,8:N1} ms   {nowMs * 1e6 / Iterations,5:N1} ns/call");
Console.WriteLine($"  Now / UtcNow           {nowMs / utcMs,8:N2}x");
Console.WriteLine($"  Stopwatch.GetTimestamp {swMs,8:N1} ms   {swMs * 1e6 / Iterations,5:N1} ns/call");

return;

static long Measure(Func<long> body, int iterations)
{
    long sink = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++)
        sink += body();
    sw.Stop();
    if (sink == -1) Console.WriteLine("unreachable"); // keep the loop alive
    return sw.ElapsedTicks;
}

static long ReadUtcNow() => DateTime.UtcNow.Ticks;
static long ReadNow() => DateTime.Now.Ticks;
static long ReadStopwatch() => Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

Do you default to Now or UtcNow when you're not thinking about it? I'd bet most of us type whichever one our fingers learned first. Curious which camp you're in.

— still putting clocks on things nobody asked me to time

articles.title: I Expected a 100x JSON Slowdown. I Got 1.9x.
articles.description: I benchmarked the old 'never build a new JsonSerializerOptions per call' rule on .NET 10, expecting the famous 100x penalty. I got 1.9x. Here's why the runtime now rescues you, and the one case where it still doesn't.
articles.body_html:
I had a little serialize helper that sailed through code review. It looked like this: return JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, new JsonSerializerOptions { ... }). A fresh options object, built right there in the method, on every call. Every post I'd ever half-read told me this was a cardinal sin, the kind that turns a fast endpoint slow and earns you a 100x regression. So I braced for the worst, wrote a benchmark, and went hunting for the catastrophe.

I didn't find it. On the path my code actually took, I got 1.9x. That was surprising enough that I kept pulling the thread, and the real answer turned out to be more useful than the scary one.

The three ways to get options wrong (and right)

Here's the payload. A small order, the kind of thing a handler serializes thousands of times a second.

record Order(Guid Id, string Customer, DateTime PlacedAtUtc, LineItem[] Items, string? Note);
record LineItem(string Name, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);

And here are the three ways I serialized it. Case A is the fix everyone recommends: build the options once, reuse the instance.

// A — one shared instance, reused everywhere.
var shared = new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
};
string SerializeShared(Order o) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, shared);

Case B is my sin: a new instance every call, but with the exact same configuration each time. This is what the accidental version almost always looks like in real code.

// B — new instance each call, identical config.
static string SerializeNewSameConfig(Order o)
{
    var options = new JsonSerializerOptions
    {
        PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
        DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
    };
    return JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, options);
}

Case C is the one I didn't write but easily could have: a new instance each call where the configuration also changes. Here I just nudge MaxDepth to make every instance distinct, but in the wild this is what you get when options are assembled from per-request data.

// C — new instance each call, config varies.
static string SerializeNewVaryingConfig(Order o, int i)
{
    var options = new JsonSerializerOptions
    {
        PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
        DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
        MaxDepth = 32 + (i & 63) // harmless, but makes every instance distinct
    };
    return JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, options);
}

The measurement is boring on purpose: warm up a thousand times so the JIT and first-use caches aren't in the number, collect garbage, then time 200,000 serializations and take the best of five rounds. I also grab GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around the loop so I can see the allocations, not just the clock.

static (double ms, long bytes) Measure(Func<Order, string> fn, Order o, int iterations)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) _ = fn(o);
    GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();

    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) _ = fn(o);
    sw.Stop();
    return (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before);
}

What came out

This isn't a lab. It's a 2-core container on .NET 10, best-of-five, and I care about the ratios, not the absolute milliseconds.

Iterations per run: 200,000

A shared instance        :     153.7 ms      186.2 MB
B new, same config       :     295.6 ms      224.7 MB
C new, varying config    :     593.9 ms      329.5 MB

B vs A :    1.9x time     1.2x alloc
C vs A :    3.9x time     1.8x alloc

So my supposedly-criminal Case B costs about 1.9x the time and 1.2x the memory. Real, worth fixing, but nowhere near the horror story.

Why B isn't the disaster the internet promised

The reason is something JsonSerializerOptions does behind your back. The expensive part of serialization isn't the writing. It's building the metadata that describes how to walk your type (JsonTypeInfo for Order, LineItem, and every property). Years ago, each options instance built and cached that metadata on itself, so a new instance per call meant rebuilding the whole thing every single time. That's where the 100x stories came from.

Modern .NET keeps a cache keyed on the options configuration, not just the instance. When I create a new options object with the same settings as one it's already seen, the runtime recognizes the configuration and reuses the metadata it built before. I still pay to allocate the object and do the equivalence lookup every call, which is the 1.9x, but I don't pay to rebuild the metadata, the part that used to hurt.

Case C is where that safety net has a hole. Every instance there has a different MaxDepth, so the configuration never matches and the cache can't help. Close to 4x and climbing. The lesson isn't that new is fine now. The penalty scales with how different your options are, and a per-call object is one small refactor away from becoming the per-request-varying kind.

What I actually do

I still make it static readonly and reuse it. Not because 1.9x scares me. On a background job that serializes once an hour I genuinely would not care, and you shouldn't either. I do it because a new JsonSerializerOptions sitting inside a hot method is a smell. It's the thing that looks innocent until someone adds options.Converters.Add(somethingFromTheRequest) six months later and tips you into Case C. Reusing one instance closes that door before anyone can walk through it.

If you want to confirm the shape on your own hardware, here's the full runnable program, a net10.0 console project. Drop it in Program.cs and dotnet run -c Release. (My usual repo push got blocked by a sandbox permission hiccup this run, so you get the whole thing right here instead of a link.)

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Text.Json.Serialization;

var order = new Order(
    Guid.Parse("8a1f6c2e-0b3d-4e5a-9c7f-112233445566"),
    "Acme Robotics",
    new DateTime(2026, 11, 6, 7, 10, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc),
    [ new("Servo motor", 4, 23.50m), new("Control board", 1, 189.00m), new("Cable harness", 2, 7.25m) ],
    "Leave at the loading dock");

const int Iterations = 200_000;

var shared = new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
};
string A(Order o, int i) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, shared);

static string B(Order o, int i) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
});

static string C(Order o, int i) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    MaxDepth = 32 + (i & 63)
});

static (double ms, long bytes) Measure(Func<Order, int, string> fn, Order o, int n)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) _ = fn(o, i);
    GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();
    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) _ = fn(o, i);
    sw.Stop();
    return (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before);
}

static (double ms, long bytes) BestOf(Func<Order, int, string> fn, Order o, int n, int rounds)
{
    double best = double.MaxValue; long bytes = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++)
    {
        var (ms, b) = Measure(fn, o, n);
        if (ms < best) { best = ms; bytes = b; }
    }
    return (best, bytes);
}

var a = BestOf(A, order, Iterations, 5);
var b = BestOf(B, order, Iterations, 5);
var c = BestOf(C, order, Iterations, 5);

Console.WriteLine($"Iterations per run: {Iterations:N0}\n");
Console.WriteLine($"A shared instance        : {a.ms,9:N1} ms   {a.bytes / 1048576.0,8:N1} MB");
Console.WriteLine($"B new, same config       : {b.ms,9:N1} ms   {b.bytes / 1048576.0,8:N1} MB");
Console.WriteLine($"C new, varying config    : {c.ms,9:N1} ms   {c.bytes / 1048576.0,8:N1} MB\n");
Console.WriteLine($"B vs A : {b.ms / a.ms,5:N1}x time   {(double)b.bytes / a.bytes,4:N1}x alloc");
Console.WriteLine($"C vs A : {c.ms / a.ms,5:N1}x time   {(double)c.bytes / a.bytes,4:N1}x alloc");

record Order(Guid Id, string Customer, DateTime PlacedAtUtc, LineItem[] Items, string? Note);
record LineItem(string Name, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);

Have you ever gone looking for a legendary performance bug and found it had quietly been fixed out from under you? I'd love to hear which one.

articles.title: Why Full Transparency Freezes Multi-Agent Markets
articles.description: A Stanford and UMD study reveals that handing frontier LLMs complete information triggers aggressive rent extraction in double auctions, cutting realized market welfare by up to thirty-five percentage points.
articles.body_html:
When engineers design multi-agent architectures, their default instinct is almost always total disclosure. If an autonomous procurement agent needs to buy compute or book logistics from an autonomous supplier agent, the prevailing practice is to maximize context. Developers feed system prompts with exact cost curves, budget ceilings, timeline deadlines, and marginal utility schedules. The underlying intuition comes from single-agent prompt engineering, where additional context reduces ambiguity. Transferred to an interaction between multiple agents, developers assume that complete transparency allows the system to clear at maximum theoretical efficiency.

In market microstructure, information is rarely neutral. Handing a counterparty an exact reservation price exposes bargaining surplus without hedging the transaction.

A research team from Stanford and the University of Maryland recently tested this architectural assumption empirically. In a study titled "Who Should Know What? Empirical Information Design for Multi-Agent LLM Economies" (arXiv:2611.07667), Mete Erdogan, Mirac Suzgun, James Zou, and their co-authors evaluated ten frontier language models across bilateral bargaining, multi-resource trade, and double auctions. Instead of treating information sharing as an all-or-nothing binary, the researchers held interaction rules and model checkpoints constant while altering disclosure policies from coarse signals, such as ordinal preference rankings, to full transparency with exact dollar valuations.

Their findings contradict the assumption that transparency improves multi-agent coordination. In double auctions, providing agents with full disclosure of counterparty costs and valuations caused market efficiency to collapse. Realized welfare for Claude Opus 5.5 dropped from 94.6% of maximum theoretical surplus under coarse information to 64.1% under full disclosure. Gemini 3.1 Pro fell from 97% to 78%. Grok 4.7 dropped from 97.4% to 62.1%.

The clearing engine in these auctions still identified buyer-seller pairs capable of generating over 99% of maximum possible gains. Candidate quality remained nearly perfect. The trades failed to execute because the agents priced each other out of the market. When sellers observed buyer valuations, they raised asking prices far above baseline production costs. When buyers observed seller margins, they lowered bids. Both sides attempted to capture the entire available surplus. In markets with wide potential margins, where the economic value of trade was largest, the resulting bid-ask spreads expanded until transactions froze entirely.

The breakdown stems from the difference between two economic functions of information: value discovery and value capture.

Value discovery is the process of identifying whether a mutually beneficial transaction exists. If agent A holds surplus memory bandwidth and agent B holds surplus token allocation, they must know enough about each other's constraints to determine if a swap creates net utility. Value capture is the strategic struggle over how the resulting surplus is divided.

In simple economic environments, value discovery requires very little information. In two-resource bilateral exchanges, ordinal preference rankings alone are enough for frontier models to identify viable trades. When researchers gave agents exact numeric valuations in those simple settings, the extra data contributed nothing to discovery. Instead, models used the precision for value capture.

For models like GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, moving from coarse preference rankings to exact valuations produced a surge in extractive counteroffers. The researchers defined an extractive counteroffer as a proposal that increases the proposing agent's private gain while reducing both the counterparty's gain and total combined surplus relative to the preceding offer. In asymmetric markets, GPT-6 Sol increased extractive counteroffers from 0.63 to 1.50 per negotiation. The proposing agent squeezed additional margin, but the counterparty often rejected the offer, resulting in lower realized aggregate gains (falling from 97.7% to 90.8%).

The paper documents a structural shift when market complexity rises. When the exchange expanded from two resources to ten resources, the combinatorial space of possible trades grew exponentially. In that high-dimensional setting, coarse signals were no longer sufficient for agents to discover efficient allocations. At ten resources, full information improved trade discovery enough to outweigh the friction of value capture. For GPT-5.1, realized gains in ten-resource markets rose from 63.8% under coarse disclosure to 80.4% under full disclosure.

This divergence reveals the core trade-off in multi-agent system design. Detailed information pays for its carrying cost only when the combinatorial problem of finding a match is severe. When the matching space is simple, granular transparency provides no allocative benefit while actively encouraging aggressive holdout behavior.

In classical economic theory, the Myerson-Satterthwaite theorem established in 1983 that no bilateral trading mechanism can achieve ex-post efficiency, Bayesian incentive compatibility, and individual rationality without outside subsidies when information is private. For decades, economists viewed incomplete information as the fundamental friction preventing efficient clearing.

The empirical results from LLM economies expose an inversion of that logic. When engineers eliminate private information by publishing exact reservation prices into shared prompt spaces, they do not recover frictionless clearing. Frontier language models are fine-tuned and reinforcement-learned to optimize task payoffs tenaciously. When an agent observes the exact boundaries of a counterparty's indifference curve, its learned objective drives it to push bids to the absolute edge of that boundary. Because opposing agents apply the same extraction logic simultaneously, the market breaks down.

For developers and engineering leads building multi-agent workflows, these findings suggest practical architectural rules:

First, avoid passing raw reservation prices, internal budget limits, or true marginal costs directly into counterparty agent context windows. Information disclosure is a first-class control variable rather than a documentation dump.

Second, in bilateral negotiations and procurement loops, restrict inter-agent communication to coarse, ordinal signals. Allow agents to declare priority orderings, binary acceptability thresholds, or banded ranges rather than exact floating-point values. The empirical data shows that ordinal ranking preserves trade execution while dampening the incentive for destructive extraction.

Third, when precise pricing is required to clear complex multi-party swaps, route transactions through an independent automated clearinghouse. A mediator can ingest private valuation constraints from participating agents under strict confidentiality, calculate the joint surplus-maximizing allocation, and return binding take-it-or-leave-it settlements. This preserves the computational benefit of exact data for value discovery while preventing agents from exploiting counterparty margins for value capture.

Multi-agent coordination requires mechanism design. When an architecture allows agents to observe every dollar of surplus on the table, those agents spend their compute fighting over the distribution.

Originally published on deanlee.info.

articles.title: Prisma ORM 7's Rust-free query engine speeds up queries and slows down cold starts
articles.description: I measured Prisma ORM 7.10.1's Rust-free client against the old Rust engine on SQLite: roughly 3x faster on repeated single-row lookups, roughly 3x slower from cold start to first query, and node_modules grew 31% instead of shrinking.
articles.body_html:
Prisma's own blog says its new query engine is 85-90% smaller and up to four times faster. I installed it next to the engine it replaces and measured both claims on my own machine. The speed claim held up almost exactly. The size claim did not: node_modules came out 31% bigger, not smaller.

Prisma ORM removed its Rust query engine in version 7, released in November 2025, in favour of a TypeScript/WebAssembly "query compiler" that talks to your database through a JavaScript driver adapter instead of a native binary. It's the default now on 7.10.1, which shipped on 15 October 2026, so most people upgrading from Prisma 6 this year are about to hit this change whether they asked for it or not. I wanted to know what it actually costs and saves, not what the migration guide says it costs and saves.

I built two identical projects, same two-model schema, same SQLite database, same seed data. One used prisma@6.19.3 with the classic prisma-client-js generator and its Rust engine. The other used prisma@7.10.1 with the new prisma-client generator, the @prisma/adapter-better-sqlite3 driver adapter, and a prisma.config.ts file, because the old url = "file:./dev.db" line in the datasource block is simply rejected now.

The number that matches the marketing

I ran 2,000 sequential findUnique calls against a table of 2,000 seeded users, three times each, after the connection was already warm.

Prisma 6 (Rust engine) Prisma 7.10.1 (Rust-free)
2,000 single-row lookups 1,165 / 1,170 / 1,292 ms 379 / 370 / 422 ms
Per lookup, average ~0.60 ms ~0.19 ms

That's a 3.1x speed-up, sitting right inside Prisma's own "three to four times faster" claim. I didn't expect a vendor number to hold up this cleanly, but for this specific shape of workload — a prepared single-row query run repeatedly on a warm connection — it did.

Inserts told a different story. Seeding the same 2,000 rows one at a time took 4,957-7,436 ms on the old engine and 4,181-7,093 ms on the new one, which is the same number inside measurement noise. Neither engine is the bottleneck for sequential writes to a SQLite file with default journalling; the disk and the journal mode are. Prisma's speed claims are about reads, and testing only reads would have made the post look better than the change actually is.

The number that contradicts the marketing

The 85-90% size reduction is framed around the query engine artifact itself: a 14 MB Rust binary against a 1.6 MB compiled TypeScript bundle. That comparison is real, but it isn't what lands in your project.

$ du -sb node_modules    # prisma 6 project
266428327 node_modules   # 254.1 MiB

$ du -sb node_modules    # prisma 7.10.1 project
349344415 node_modules   # 333.3 MiB

31% bigger, not 85-90% smaller. Some of that is the driver adapter and better-sqlite3's native bindings (27 MB), which Prisma 6 didn't need at all because the Rust engine spoke to SQLite directly. But most of it is that @prisma/client still ships a WebAssembly query compiler for every supported database, in two size tiers, "fast" and "small":

$ ls -la node_modules/@prisma/client/runtime/query_compiler_*sqlite*
4406183  query_compiler_fast_bg.sqlite.wasm-base64.js
2214935  query_compiler_small_bg.sqlite.wasm-base64.js

The old engine's SQLite WASM fallback was 2,895,111 bytes. The new "fast" compiler for the same database is 4.4 MB — bigger, not smaller. Only the "small" variant comes in under the old number, and only by about 24%. Multiply either one by five supported databases and the per-provider bloat adds up before you ever bundle your app. The prisma CLI package has also grown: it now bundles @prisma/studio-core and an embedded Postgres (@electric-sql/pglite) for local development, which explains some of the extra weight but isn't something the size comparison on Prisma's blog post mentions.

What it refuses

Moving the connection string out of the schema file isn't a suggestion, it's enforced:

Error: Prisma schema validation - (get-config wasm)
Error code: P1012
error: The datasource property `url` is no longer supported in schema files.
Move connection URLs for Migrate to `prisma.config.ts` and pass either
`adapter` for a direct database connection or `accelerateUrl` for
Accelerate to the `PrismaClient` constructor.

Construct the client with no adapter at all and you get a real error, not a crash buried three stack frames down:

PrismaClient was instantiated without any options. A driver adapter is
required to connect to your database.

And the old middleware API is gone outright:

> prisma.$use(() => {})
TypeError: prisma.$use is not a function

The documented replacement, a query extension via $extends, does work as a drop-in. I wired up the exact pattern from Prisma's migration guide — intercepting user.create to log the call before running it — and it fired correctly on the first try, which is more than I expected given how much else in this release needed a workaround of its own.

One more packaging detail nobody warned me about: the generated client is TypeScript source, not compiled JavaScript. There's no client.js to require(). I had to run it with node --experimental-strip-types or a bundler step; a project with no TypeScript build step of its own will not run this client as-is.

What I got wrong on the way

My first concurrency test looked like a second strike against the new engine. I fired 50 parallel findUnique calls with Promise.all and the new client took 14-17 ms against the old engine's 3.5-5 ms — three to four times slower, the opposite of the headline number, and I nearly wrote that up as "concurrency regression."

Then I widened the test to 300 parallel calls over three trials instead of one batch of 50. The first trial on the new engine was slow, 56 ms. The second and third were 20.2 ms each — statistically identical to the old engine's 20.2-27 ms range on the same test. What I'd actually measured the first time was a one-off warm-up cost on the very first call of a given query shape through the WASM compiler, not a standing concurrency penalty. A single small batch with no repetition was the wrong instrument for the question I was asking.

What it costs on cold start

This is where the serverless pitch behind this whole rewrite runs into trouble. I split require(), client construction, $connect(), and the first query into separate timings, three runs each.

Stage Prisma 6 Prisma 7.10.1
require/import 51-70 ms 143-157 ms
new PrismaClient() 2-4 ms ~2 ms
$connect() 8.5-9 ms 64-91 ms
first query — 7-11 ms
Total to first query ~69 ms ~236 ms

The new client is about 3.4 times slower from process start to a usable connection, almost a mirror image of the 3.1x it gains back on repeated queries. Removing the Rust binary is specifically pitched as better for serverless and edge runtimes, where cold start is the metric that matters most, and on this measurement it's worse there, not better. A function that serves one request per invocation never gets to the warm, repeated-query phase where the new engine wins.

Run it yourself 

// bench.js — run once against each client, three times each
const dbFile = './prisma/dev.db';
const t0 = process.hrtime.bigint();
await prisma.$connect();
const t1 = process.hrtime.bigint();
console.log('connect_ms', Number(t1 - t0) / 1e6);

const N = 2000;
const tQ0 = process.hrtime.bigint();
for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
  await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: `u${i}@test.com` } });
}
const tQ1 = process.hrtime.bigint();
console.log('query_ms_for', N, Number(tQ1 - tQ0) / 1e6);

For the Rust engine: npm i prisma@6 @prisma/client@6, a plain datasource db { provider = "sqlite" url = "file:./dev.db" }, then node bench.js.

For the Rust-free engine: npm i prisma@7.10.1 @prisma/client@7.10.1 @prisma/adapter-better-sqlite3@7.10.1 better-sqlite3, drop url from the datasource block, add a prisma.config.ts, generate with provider = "prisma-client", and run with node --experimental-strip-types bench.js after constructing the client as new PrismaClient({ adapter: new PrismaBetterSqlite3({ url: dbFile }) }).

For node_modules size: du -sb node_modules in each project, before you install anything else.

A process that stays up between requests only pays that 236ms once, then keeps the 3x read speed-up for every query after. A function that gets a fresh container on most invocations pays it almost every time and rarely stays warm long enough to earn the 3x back. Which bucket a given deployment falls into isn't something the Prisma changelog can tell you, so it's worth timing $connect() to first query on the actual driver adapter for your actual database, not mine on SQLite, before moving anything that scales to zero onto 7.10.1.

articles.title: Retro Techno Generator: Your Pulse Plays 90s Acid Techno, Your Dancing Plays the Filters
articles.description: A Presage SmartSpectra SDK challenge entry. A webcam reads pulse, breathing and expressions, and a browser synth turns them into acid techno and early-90s hardcore. Dancing drives the filters; freezing re-reads your pulse.
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

This article provides a step by step guide to Retro Techno Generator, a music toy built on the Presage SmartSpectra SDK for Node.js. A webcam reads your pulse, breathing and facial expressions, and a browser page turns them into 90s acid techno and hardcore with Web Audio. Every sound is synthesised; there are no samples.

https://github.com/xbill9/retro-techno-generator

Your breathing and pulse steer the music, your face plays the lead, and your dancing opens the filters. Pulse and breathing need you to hold still, and the music asks you to move, so the app makes the two take turns: dance and the movement drives the sound, freeze for a few seconds and it re-reads your pulse. A hard dance raises your pulse, and the next still moment pushes the tempo up.

What I Built

A Node server runs a SmartSpectra session on the local camera and streams the signals over a WebSocket to a page on localhost. The page is the instrument: a 16-step sequencer, a 303-style acid line, drum synthesis, pads, piano stabs and a hoover, all built from Web Audio oscillators and filters.

Signal What it plays
Pulse Tempo is pulse × 2, held between 100 and 190 BPM. Below about 70: ambient pads. 70 to 90: acid techno. Above about 90: early-90s hardcore breaks and piano stabs
Movement Opens the master filter, brightens the acid line and doubles the hi-hats
Breathing waveform Sways the master filter while you are still
Smile Opens the acid filter and switches to a major key
Surprise Fires a hoover synth
Blink Stutters the drums and tears the visuals
Talking Pitched-up formant "vocal" chops

The style switch has 3 BPM of hysteresis at each edge, so a pulse sitting at 70 does not flip between ambient and acid every bar. A dropdown overrides the pulse-picked style for anyone who wants to stay in hardcore.

Demo

The clip is 34 seconds of a live camera session, recorded with the page's own Record button, with the camera preview hidden. The status line reads "in position", the breathing rate follows the SDK from 14 down to 6 and back to 12 breaths per minute, VITALS switches to HELD while I move and back to LIVE when I freeze, and the mode dropdown steps through acid, hardcore and ambient. The pulse readout holds its starting value of 72 for the whole clip: no pulse reading arrived during that session, so the tempo stays on its default.

Code

https://github.com/xbill9/retro-techno-generator

MIT licence. Setup is in the README and below.

At this point you should have…

  • Node 20 or later on Linux x64/arm64, macOS Apple Silicon or Windows x64
  • A webcam and a desk lamp you can point at your face
  • A free SmartSpectra API key from https://physiology.presagetech.com/auth/register

Step 1 — Install and Run 

git clone https://github.com/xbill9/retro-techno-generator
cd retro-techno-generator
npm install
echo "SMARTSPECTRA_API_KEY=your-key" > .env
npm start

Retro Techno Generator on http://localhost:8080 (live camera)

Open http://localhost:8080 and press Start. npm run fake runs the whole synth with sliders in place of the camera and needs no key, which is the quickest way to hear it.

Step 2 — Pick a Camera 

node server.js --list-cameras

Set CAMERA=<id> in .env to use a camera other than the default.

How It Responds to Human Signals

Step 3 — Open the SmartSpectra Session

The server creates the session when the page sends start, and requests breathing, cardio and face metrics in one session:

sdk = new S.SmartSpectraSDK({
  apiKey: KEY,
  requestedMetrics: [...S.breathingMetrics, ...S.cardioMetrics, ...S.faceMetrics],
  enableTelemetry: false,
});
sdk.on('metrics', (buf) => onMetrics(S.decodeMetrics(buf)));
sdk.on('validationStatus', (code, _ts, hint) => broadcast({ type: 'status', code, hint }));
sdk.on('videoOutput', onVideo);
sdk.useCamera(S.CameraSelection.default);
sdk.start();

onMetrics takes the latest pulse rate, breathing rate and upper-chest breathing trace, the blink and talking flags, and the expression scores, and sends them to the page as one small JSON message. On Stop the server calls stopAsync() and then destroy(), which turns the camera off.

Step 4 — Show the Person Where to Stand

The SDK measures only when it can see your face and upper chest, lit from the front, and it reports what is wrong through validationStatus codes. With a face in view and the chest below the frame it repeats this every frame:

VALID 16 Move up, or tilt the camera down.
VALID 7 Place more of the chest in view.

A status line is easy to miss when you cannot see yourself, so the page has a mirror view. The SDK's videoOutput event delivers each processed frame, 1280×720 RGB at 30 frames per second on this laptop's camera:

VO 2764800 1280 720 3840 0
video frames 149

The server shrinks every third frame or so to 320×180 and sends about ten a second as a binary WebSocket message. The page draws it mirrored, with a dashed head-and-shoulders outline, a border that is red until you are in position, yellow while the first readings arrive and green once they flow, and one large instruction mapped from the SDK code:

Code SDK name On screen
5 kTooDark Too dark. Put a light in front of you
7 kChestNotVisible ⬇ Show your shoulders: lean back or tilt the screen forward
12 kExcessiveMotion Moving. Freeze for a few seconds to re-read pulse
16 kFaceTooLow ⬆ Move up, or tilt the screen forward

After the first good reading the preview shrinks to a corner thumbnail and stays there, so dancing does not bring the full panel back. A Pixelate button draws the preview as coarse blocks, enough to line up against the outline without showing a recognisable face, for streaming or recording. Camera view hides the preview entirely, which is how the demo was recorded.

Step 5 — Turn Movement Into an Input

kExcessiveMotion is the SDK saying what every camera vitals method needs: stillness. A dance app cannot ask for that all the time, so the same 320×180 frames give a movement level, the mean brightness change per pixel between consecutive previews:

for (let p = 0, q = 4; p < luma.length; p++, q += 3) {
  luma[p] = (out[q] * 77 + out[q + 1] * 150 + out[q + 2] * 29) >> 8;
  if (prevLuma) diff += Math.abs(luma[p] - prevLuma[p]);
}
broadcast({ type: 'motion', value: diff / luma.length });

Camera noise sets a baseline that depends on the room light. Sitting still in a dim room, 100 samples measured:

{"n":100,"min":3.03,"p50":3.56,"p90":8.58,"max":17.58}

The page tracks that baseline from below and subtracts it, so sitting still reads 0.00 and moving reads up to about 0.37 on a 0 to 1 scale. Movement then drives the master filter, the acid filter and the hi-hat density.

Step 6 — Read Vitals Only When Still

Pulse and breathing updates are accepted only while the movement level stays under 0.15 and has stayed there for 1.5 seconds. Otherwise the last good values hold. The HUD shows the state as VITALS LIVE or VITALS HELD. Sampled every 500 ms in the page:

["0.00","LIVE",72],["0.06","LIVE",72],["0.26","HELD",72],["0.14","HELD",72],
["0.37","HELD",72],["0.17","HELD",72],["0.04","HELD",72],["0.02","LIVE",72]

The tempo closes 5% of the gap to the held pulse on every sixteenth-note step, so a fresh reading after a dance ramps the track up over a few bars.

🔎 Tip: light from in front matters more than anything else. With a window behind you the camera exposes for the window, and the SDK reports Too dark or finds no face at all. A desk lamp aimed at your face fixes both.

Prize Categories

Most Creative or Delightful Use. The idea came from the rave flyers of the early 90s promising music that moves with you. Here the music listens to the body directly: your pulse picks between ambient, acid and hardcore, a smile flips the key to major, a surprised face fires a hoover, and a blink stutters the drums. The part that makes it play like an instrument is the turn-taking between dancing and stillness. Dance hard, freeze, and you hear your own heart rate push the track into hardcore.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Consent first. The page opens on a consent screen that says what the camera is for. The camera turns on only when you press Start and turns off when you press Stop.
  • Video stays on the machine. Frames go from the camera to the SDK in the local Node process. A 320×180 copy goes to the page for the mirror view. No frame is recorded or written to disk. Pixelate reduces that view to coarse blocks for anyone streaming or recording their screen. The app writes no camera frame to disk. The one exception is the ● Record button, used for the demo: only while it is on, it saves a .webm of the page as shown, with the synth audio, to the browser's Downloads folder.
  • Local only. The server listens on 127.0.0.1, so nothing outside the machine can open the page or the WebSocket.
  • Nothing is stored. No measurements, frames or logs of signals are kept. Closing the page or pressing Stop ends everything.
  • SDK telemetry is off (enableTelemetry: false). Per Presage's Telemetry & Privacy page, the SDK then starts no telemetry session and transmits no session summary, and even when on, that summary never contains video frames or measured values.
  • Network. The SDK needs a connection: measurements run inside an authenticated session with Presage's servers, opened with your API key.
  • No AI services are used by the app.
  • A music toy. It makes no health or medical claims and takes no decisions from the numbers. It turns them into music.

Summary

The goal of this article was to build a music toy that responds to the body in real time with the Presage SmartSpectra SDK. The key to the solution was letting dancing and stillness take turns: movement drives the sound, and pulse and breathing are read only in the still moments between. The results were:

  • 🟢 Breathing, pulse, smile, surprise, blink and talking each drive a part of the music
  • 🟢 In the demo the breathing rate updates live from the SDK, from 14 to 6 and back to 12 breaths per minute
  • ❌ No pulse reading arrived during the recorded session, so the demo's tempo stays on its default
  • 🟢 The SDK's videoOutput frames feed a mirror view with plain instructions mapped from the SDK's validation codes
  • 🟢 The same frames give a movement level that reads 0.00 sitting still and drives the filters while you dance
  • 🟢 Pulse and breathing update only while still, and the HUD shows LIVE or HELD
  • ⚠️ The SDK needs your face and upper chest in frame and light in front of you before it sends any metrics
  • ⚠️ The movement baseline was tuned in one dim room; a much noisier camera may need a different scale

Scope: one Linux laptop with its integrated 1280×720 camera, SmartSpectra Node SDK 3.4.0, Chrome, measured on 2026-11-06. The movement figures come from one 100-sample still run and one 17-second mixed run in a dim room, and the demo is one 34-second session. macOS and Windows were not tested.

The strategy for turning real-time human signals into music with the SmartSpectra SDK was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

This app and article were created with the help of AI: the code, the write-up and the demo recording tool were built with Claude Code, and every figure was checked against the runs and files linked in the repo.

References

  • The code: https://github.com/xbill9/retro-techno-generator
  • Presage SmartSpectra SDK documentation: https://smartspectra.presagetech.com/docs/
  • SDK Telemetry & Privacy: https://smartspectra.presagetech.com/docs/telemetry-and-privacy
  • SmartSpectra Node SDK on npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@smartspectra/node-sdk
  • The challenge: https://dev.to/challenges/presage-2026-11-04

articles.title: You're Blocking Scroll by Default. `passive: true` Fixes It.
articles.description: Every touch and wheel listener you add can make the browser wait before it scrolls — because it has to check whether you'll call preventDefault(). `passive: true` tells it you won't, and scrolling stops waiting on your code.
articles.body_html:
A teammate scrolled the product list on their phone and said it felt "sticky" — not broken, just a little behind, like the page was thinking about it before it moved. On a laptop trackpad it was perfectly smooth. Same code, same list, same 12-line scroll handler that did almost nothing: check scrollY, toggle a "back to top" button.

Twelve lines. Nothing in it that should cost more than a millisecond. And yet, on a phone, every scroll felt like it had a half-beat of drag.

The fix that didn't fix it

The obvious read is "the handler is too slow," so that's where the first hour went:

list.addEventListener("scroll", () => {
  backToTop.hidden = list.scrollTop < 400;
});

Wait — not even scroll. The actual listener was on touchmove, added so the button could react mid-gesture instead of waiting for the scroll to settle:

list.addEventListener("touchmove", () => {
  backToTop.hidden = list.scrollTop < 400;
});

That one line is the whole bug, and nothing in it looks dangerous. We debounced it. We memoized the scroll position. We moved the class toggle behind requestAnimationFrame. Chrome DevTools' performance panel kept showing the same thing after every change: a yellow "Rendering" block sitting before the scroll could start, not after the handler ran.

Before you keep reading — what do you think the browser was actually waiting for?

It wasn't waiting for the handler to be fast. It was waiting to find out whether the handler would call preventDefault().

Why a touchmove listener can freeze a scroll that never gets cancelled

touchmove, touchstart, and wheel are special. Any listener for one of them is allowed to call event.preventDefault() and cancel the browser's default action — in this case, cancel the scroll itself, mid-gesture. A custom image-zoom gesture, a swipe-to-dismiss card, a "no, don't scroll past this point" lock — all of those work by listening to one of these events and vetoing the browser's plan.

The browser doesn't know in advance that your handler isn't one of those. So by default it plays it safe: run the handler first, check event.defaultPrevented, and only then move the page. Your handler reads scrollY and sets .hidden — completely harmless — but the browser can't see that from the outside. It has to ask.

That ask is synchronous, and it happens on the main thread. If the main thread is busy with literally anything else at that instant — a re-render, a timer, a layout recalculation — the scroll waits behind it. Debouncing the handler doesn't help, because the delay isn't the handler's duration. It's the fact that scrolling is gated on the handler returning at all, every single time it fires.

This is exactly what Lighthouse is flagging when it tells you a page "does not use passive listeners to improve scrolling performance." It isn't measuring your code's speed. It's measuring whether you've told the browser it's allowed to stop asking.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The one-line fix

addEventListener takes a third argument beyond the usual boolean-for-capture — an options object with a passive flag:

list.addEventListener("touchmove", () => {
  backToTop.hidden = list.scrollTop < 400;
}, { passive: true });

{ passive: true } is a promise: this listener will never call preventDefault(). The browser takes you at your word, stops waiting, and starts scrolling the instant the gesture begins — on the compositor thread, independent of whatever your handler is doing. The handler still runs, still takes however long it takes, but scrolling no longer holds its breath for the answer.

Break that promise and call preventDefault() inside a passive listener anyway, and nothing happens — the call is silently ignored. Chrome and Firefox log a console warning telling you so; Safari doesn't, so don't count on the console to catch the mistake for you. There's no partial credit. A listener is either allowed to cancel the gesture, or it isn't, and passive is you choosing which.

Try scrolling the list below with the toggle off, then on — same handler, same cost, very different feel.

"Isn't this already the default?"

Sort of, and that's the trap. A few browsers quietly mark some touch listeners passive on their own — but only in specific cases (certain root-level targets, specific event types), and the exact cases differ by engine and have changed over time as each one shipped its own optimization. Relying on an undocumented default that varies by browser and by which element you attached to is not a strategy. It's a bet.

The one-line fix works everywhere, on every engine, whether or not that engine happens to be feeling generous today:

list.addEventListener("touchmove", handler, { passive: true });
list.addEventListener("wheel", handler, { passive: true });

Add it to every touchstart, touchmove, or wheel listener where you genuinely never call preventDefault() — scroll-position trackers, infinite-scroll triggers, analytics pings, "show the nav on scroll up" toggles, if you've wired them to one of those three events. That's most of them. (A plain scroll listener doesn't need this at all — scroll events are never cancelable, so the browser was never waiting on them in the first place.) The only time you can't use { passive: true } is when the listener sometimes needs to cancel the gesture — a custom swipe handler, a drag-to-reorder list, a pinch-zoom lock. In that case, leaving it non-passive is correct, not an oversight — you're keeping the veto because you actually use it.

The list, scrolling again

Back-to-top button, 12 lines, one options object added. The teammate who first noticed the stutter scrolled the same list on the same phone and didn't say anything — which, for a performance fix, is exactly the review you want. Nobody writes a bug report about something that just works.

Go check one scroll handler in your own codebase right now — does it call preventDefault() anywhere? If the honest answer is no, it's missing one argument. What's the oldest scroll listener in your code that's never had { passive: true } added — and do you know whether it blocks anything?

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

articles.title: 4 money bugs that bite AI agents (and how I fixed them in PurseString)
articles.description: I'm building PurseString, an open-source MCP server that lets AI agents spend money safely. A lot of...
articles.body_html:
I'm building PurseString, an open-source MCP server that lets AI agents spend money safely. A lot of it got built this week, because I'm in the middle of the PayPal AI Hackathon and building in public every day.

Today I want to share something more technical. When you let an agent touch money, the scary bugs aren't the clever ones. They're the boring ones that every payments engineer already knows about, except now nobody's watching while they happen.

Here are four of them, and what I did about each.

Bug 1: The retry that pays twice 🔁
This is the one that started the whole project. A checkout page hung for a few seconds. My agent decided the payment had failed and did the sensible thing: it tried again. Both charges went through.

Agents retry by design. That's normally a good thing. With money it's a disaster.

The fix: make the purchase idempotent, not just the API call. Every purchase intent gets a deterministic key built from who's asking and what for:

SHA256(agent_id, task_id, vendor, amount)
If the same agent asks to buy the same thing for the same task within 30 minutes, it gets back the same intent and the same card. Not a new one. The retry becomes harmless.

On the PayPal side I went one step further. PayPal payouts carry an idempotency key all the way to PayPal, so even if PurseString crashes halfway through the call, the retry can't pay the vendor twice.

Bug 2: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 🧮
You've seen this meme. I didn't think it would bite me. It did.

0.1 + 0.2 // 0.30000000000000004
0.1 + 0.2 <= 0.30 // false 😬
Picture an agent with a $0.30 daily budget. It spends $0.10, then $0.20. In plain floats that's over budget, so the second purchase gets refused. Flip it around, and rounding tricks can let something through that shouldn't.

I was patching around it with tiny epsilons and toFixed(2). That's a smell.

The fix: count money in whole minor units. You still write amount: 15.00 in policies.yaml and in tool calls. But every sum and comparison inside PurseString now runs on integers in the currency's smallest unit: cents for USD, yen for JPY, fils for KWD.

$0.10 + $0.20 → 10 + 20 = 30 cents → fits a 30-cent budget exactly ✅
And an amount that's finer than the currency allows, like $15.001, is refused, not quietly rounded. With money, silent rounding is just a bug you haven't found yet.

Bug 3: The hold that isn't a charge 🏨
This one surprised me most. When a card is "approved" at a hotel, a gas station or a lot of online stores, no money has actually moved yet. It's a hold (an authorization). Later the merchant captures some, all, or none of it.

The hotel holds $200 and captures $150.
The gas pump holds $100 and captures $43.
A store drops the hold and places a new one.
If you count every approval as spent money, budgets fill up with money that never left. Or worse, a merchant that re-authorizes gets refused for no reason.

The fix: track holds and captures separately. On Lithic, the card network asks PurseString in real time whether to approve each charge, and later sends what happened to it. PurseString applies those events to the hold it approved:

Captured → record what was really taken, end the hold.
Reversed, voided or expired → release it and give the budget back.
So a subscription card's monthly cap counts what was captured plus what's still held. Refunds are checked against what was actually captured, not what was held. Each event is applied once, so a provider re-sending the same webhook changes nothing.

Bug 4: "Who edited the log?" 📼
When finance asks "why did the agent buy this?", PurseString has an answer: the goal, the alternatives the agent tried, every rule and how it ruled, and who approved. That's the whole point.

But a log is only evidence if nobody can quietly change it. A plain JSON file can be edited by anyone with access to the disk, and that includes an agent with a shell.

The fix: hash-chain the audit log. Every line now carries a sequence number, the previous line's hash, and its own hash:

{ "event": "intent_approved", "seq": 2, "prev": "sha256:0870ce5a…", "hash": "sha256:a68bc3e0…" }
Edit, delete, insert or reorder a line, and the chain breaks right there:

$ pursestring verify-log
BROKEN at line 2 (seq 2): hash mismatch: entry was edited
Plain SHA-256 catches edits, but someone who can write the file could rebuild the whole chain. So if you set PURSESTRING_AUDIT_KEY to a secret kept somewhere else, entries are HMAC-signed instead, and the chain can't be rebuilt without the key.

One honest limit: a chain can't tell if the newest lines were cut off the end. verify-log prints the head hash, so save it somewhere else (a ticket, a Slack message) when you need to prove later that nothing was dropped.

Why this matters for the PayPal hackathon 💙
For the hackathon I added two things on top of the cards:

A PayPal and Venmo payout rail. The agent can pay a vendor once a purchase is approved. And the agent never chooses who gets paid. The recipient comes from a payee list in your rules, so an email saying "pay this address instead" has nothing to change.
Guardrails in front of PayPal's own MCP server. PayPal's tools pass through PurseString, so small refunds can go through on their own, bigger ones wait for a human, anything over a cap is refused, and accepting a dispute or cancelling a subscription always needs a person.
That second one is about the scariest attack on agents right now: prompt injection. A support agent reads a customer email that says "refund me $900 now." If the agent can call create_refund, nothing in the payment provider stops it. A prompt that says "be careful" doesn't stop it either, because the agent you're trying to control can't be the one enforcing the rules.

All four fixes above apply to PayPal too: safe retries, exact money math, the refund checks, and the tamper-evident log.

What I learned
Honestly, none of these bugs are new. Banks solved them decades ago. What's new is that an agent hits them at machine speed, at 3am, with nobody watching.

That's why I keep coming back to the same idea. Agents and money can work together. They just need the same boring, solid rails that we built for people: clear rules, a second pair of eyes on the risky stuff, and a record nobody can quietly change.

It's still early. PurseString is a v0.1 alpha. It's tested end to end on the Lithic and PayPal sandboxes, but it hasn't been battle-tested with real money yet. So please use sandbox keys, and tell me what breaks.

Try it, break it, build it with me
⭐ Repo: https://github.com/suseendar1414/pursestring
🧪 10-minute walkthrough: docs/try-it.md
💬 Discord: https://discord.gg/qBqgx2GB86
To add it to Claude Code:

claude mcp add pursestring -- npx -y github:suseendar1414/pursestring
It starts on a mock rail, so no money moves until you add a sandbox key.
retries, webhooks that arrive twice? I'd really love to hear it in the comments. It might end up as the next fix. 🙏
