Testing Electron Apps: A Practical Guide to Unit, Integration, and E2E Coverage

TL;DR: Electron apps are not just web apps — they are Node main processes, sandboxed renderers, a preload bridge, and an OS-native surface. Testing them with only a Vitest config and a hope will leave your IPC contracts and window lifecycle untested. This post lays out the four-layer testing strategy we actually ship with: unit tests for main-process logic, component tests for the renderer, IPC contract tests that lock the preload boundary, and Playwright E2E that launches the real Electron binary. It also tells you what not to test, so you don't spend three days fighting native dialogs.

Table of Contents

  1. Why Electron testing is different
  2. Layer 1 — Unit tests for main-process logic
  3. Layer 2 — Component tests for the renderer
  4. Layer 3 — IPC contract tests
  5. Layer 4 — E2E with Playwright
  6. What not to test
  7. Pitfalls we hit in production
  8. Checklist

Why Electron testing is different

A browser-only web app has one process and one event loop. An Electron app has at least:

  • a main process running Node.js (window lifecycle, file system, menus, tray);
  • one or more renderer processes running your web UI (sandboxed, no direct Node access);
  • a preload script that bridges the two via contextBridge;
  • and a pile of OS-native bits (dialogs, notifications, global shortcuts, auto-updater).

Each of these layers needs a different testing approach. If you only run renderer unit tests, your IPC handlers are untested. If you only run E2E, every test takes 20 seconds and you will delete the suite the first time it flakes. The goal is a pyramid: lots of fast tests at the bottom, a thin layer of slow E2E at the top.

Layer 1 — Unit tests for main-process logic

Main-process code should be plain TypeScript modules that take dependencies as arguments, not modules that import electron at the top level and call BrowserWindow.getAllWindows() on import. That shape is what makes it testable.

// src/main/project-service.ts
import { promises as fs } from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';

export interface ProjectRepo {
  root: string;
}

export class ProjectService {
  constructor(private readonly fsImpl: typeof fs = fs) {}

  async listRecent(repo: ProjectRepo, limit = 10): Promise<string[]> {
    const entries = await this.fsImpl.readdir(repo.root, { withFileTypes: true });
    return entries
      .filter((e) => e.isDirectory())
      .map((e) => e.name)
      .slice(0, limit);
  }

  async ensureProjectDir(repo: ProjectRepo, name: string): Promise<string> {
    const dir = path.join(repo.root, name);
    await this.fsImpl.mkdir(dir, { recursive: true });
    return dir;
  }
}

The fsImpl injection is the trick. In production you pass the real fs; in tests you pass an in-memory stub.

// test/main/project-service.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { ProjectService } from '../../src/main/project-service';

function fakeFs(dirs: string[]) {
  return {
    readdir: async () => dirs.map((name) => ({ name, isDirectory: () => true })),
    mkdir: async () => undefined,
  } as any;
}

describe('ProjectService', () => {
  it('lists up to limit directories', async () => {
    const svc = new ProjectService(fakeFs(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']));
    const out = await svc.listRecent({ root: '/repo' }, 2);
    expect(out).toEqual(['a', 'b']);
  });
});

Run this with plain vitest run — no Electron binary, no display. It should finish in milliseconds.

Rule: Anything in src/main that does not touch BrowserWindow, app, or native modules should be importable under plain Node. If importing it requires a running Electron, you have coupled your business logic to the framework and need to refactor.

Layer 2 — Component tests for the renderer

The renderer is just a web app, so you already know how to test it: Vitest + your component testing library of choice. The only Electron-specific twist is that window.electron (your contextBridge exposure) does not exist in the test environment. Stub it globally.

// test/renderer/setup.ts
beforeEach(() => {
  (window as any).electron = {
    projects: {
      list: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue([{ name: 'demo', path: '/p/demo' }]),
      create: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue('/p/demo'),
    },
    shell: { openExternal: vi.fn() },
  };
});

Then your component tests look exactly like web tests:

import { render, screen, fireEvent } from '@testing-library/react';
import { ProjectList } from '../../src/renderer/components/ProjectList';

it('renders projects from the IPC bridge', async () => {
  render(<ProjectList />);
  expect(await screen.findByText('demo')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

it('calls create when the new-project button is clicked', async () => {
  render(<ProjectList />);
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /new project/i }));
  expect(window.electron.projects.create).toHaveBeenCalled();
});

The benefit of stubbing at window.electron rather than mocking your own wrapper is that the preload contract is what you are testing against — if you rename a method in preload and forget to update the renderer, TypeScript will still compile because the stub is any, but Layer 3 below will catch it.

Layer 3 — IPC contract tests

This is the layer most teams skip, and it is the one that catches real bugs. The preload script is a contract between untrusted renderer code and privileged main-process code. Test that contract explicitly.

// test/ipc/contract.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { contextBridge, ipcRenderer } from 'electron';

// We import the real preload source and run it against a fake contextBridge.
let exposed: Record<string, unknown> = {};
(contextBridge as any).exposeInMainWorld = (key: string, api: unknown) => {
  exposed[key] = api;
};
(ipcRenderer as any).invoke = async (channel: string, ...args: unknown[]) => {
  return { channel, args };
};

// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-var-requires
require('../../src/preload/index.ts');

describe('preload contract', () => {
  it('exposes a typed projects API', () => {
    expect(exposed).toHaveProperty('electron.projects');
    const api = (exposed as any).electron;
    expect(typeof api.projects.list).toBe('function');
    expect(typeof api.projects.create).toBe('function');
    expect(typeof api.shell.openExternal).toBe('function');
  });

  it('does not leak raw ipcRenderer onto the bridge', () => {
    expect((exposed as any).electron).not.toHaveProperty('ipcRenderer');
  });

  it('routes list to the expected channel', async () => {
    const api = (exposed as any).electron;
    const res = await api.projects.list();
    expect(res.channel).toBe('projects:list');
  });
});

The three assertions that matter:

  1. Every method you expect is exposed — renaming or dropping one breaks the build.
  2. Raw ipcRenderer is not on the bridge — a common security slip.
  3. Channel names match what ipcMain.handle registers — pair this with a test on the main side that enumerates registered handlers and asserts they are in the allowlist.

We also keep a single src/shared/ipc-channels.ts that exports channel name constants, and both preload and main import from it. No stringly-typed channels scattered across the codebase.

Layer 4 — E2E with Playwright

Unit and contract tests give you confidence in individual pieces. E2E gives you confidence that the real Electron binary, the real preload, and the real main process work together. Playwright has first-class Electron support, and you should use it.

// e2e/app.spec.ts
import { test, expect, _electron as electron } from '@playwright/test';
import { join } from 'node:path';

test('window opens and shows the project list', async () => {
  const app = await electron.launch({
    args: [join(__dirname, '..', '..', 'out', 'main', 'index.js')],
  });
  const win = await app.firstWindow();
  await win.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

  await expect(win.locator('h1')).toContainText('Projects');
  await expect(win.locator('[data-testid="project-list"] .project')).toHaveCount(1);

  // exercise an IPC round-trip through the real bridge
  await win.getByRole('button', { name: /new project/i }).click();
  await expect(win.locator('.project')).toHaveCount(2);

  await app.close();
});

A few things we learned the hard way:

  • Launch the built output, not electron . against source. Use your compiled out/main/index.js so the E2E is testing what you actually ship.
  • Use app.firstWindow() rather than guessing a URL. Electron windows do not have a useful URL for your main window in packaged builds.
  • waitForLoadState is your friend. Rushing assertions after launch is the #1 cause of flakes.
  • Give each E2E test a clean user-data dir via --user-data-dir=$TMPDIR/... so tests do not share state.
  • Do not click native OS dialogs from Playwright. If your flow opens a dialog.showOpenDialog, stub it from the main process in test mode (see next section).

What not to test

Some things look testable but are not worth the maintenance cost.

Surface Why skip it What to do instead
Native dialog.showOpenDialog / showMessageBox OS-level, platform-specific, unscriptable reliably Inject a dialogService interface; use a stub in tests
Auto-updater network calls Depends on external server, signed updates, real code signatures Unit-test the decision logic (should update? roll back?), never autoUpdater.checkForUpdates()
Tray icon rendering Pure OS compositor Screenshot once manually; do not assert pixels
Global shortcuts Hook into the OS input stack Test the registration/unregistration logic, not the keypress itself
Code signing / notarization External, slow, network-bound Verify on CI with a single dedicated job, not in PR tests
Crash reporter native dumps Requires an actual crash Unit-test the breadcrumb/redaction layer; send one real crash to staging manually

The pattern: test your logic, not the operating system. Wrap the native call behind a tiny interface, test your code that decides what to call, and let the integration points be covered by Layer 4 smoke tests only.

Pitfalls we hit in production

  1. __dirname is not what you expect in ESM builds. Electron has migrated to ESM; if your Playwright launch path is relative, you will silently start the wrong bundle. Use path.join(__dirname, ...) explicitly and log the resolved path in CI.
  2. Preload changes do not hot-reload. When you change src/preload, you must rebuild and restart Electron. Stale preloads are the #1 "works in unit, fails in E2E" bug.
  3. Sandbox enabled means your preload runs in a more restricted context. Node builtins you used in preload will not be available. Keep preload minimal — IPC channel names and argument validation only.
  4. Renderer fetch to local files is blocked by CSP. E2E tests that load file:// resources need the same CSP you ship in production, or you will green-test a broken build.
  5. Playwright and Electron versions must match. A Playwright built for Electron 30 will flake on Electron 33. Pin them together.
  6. app.getPath('userData') is shared across test runs. Two E2E tests writing to the same SQLite file will corrupt each other. Pass a fresh --user-data-dir per test worker.

Checklist

  • [ ] Business logic in src/main imports no electron module at the top level
  • [ ] Main-process services accept their Node dependencies as constructor args
  • [ ] Renderer tests stub window.electron in a global setup file
  • [ ] A contract test enumerates every method on the preload bridge and asserts raw ipcRenderer is not exposed
  • [ ] IPC channel names live in a single shared constants module
  • [ ] E2E launches the built output, not source
  • [ ] Every E2E worker gets a fresh --user-data-dir
  • [ ] Native dialogs and auto-updater are behind interfaces with test doubles
  • [ ] CI runs unit + contract on every PR, E2E on every push to main
  • [ ] Playwright and Electron major versions are pinned together

Testing Electron well is less about choosing a framework and more about drawing the process boundaries clearly. Once your main logic is plain Node, your renderer is a plain web app, and your preload is a tiny testable contract, the actual test files are almost boring — which is exactly what you want.

articles.title: How I Made AI Characters Follow the Cursor
articles.description: A practical look at the videos, frame maps, browser fixes, costs, and failed attempts behind cursor-following AI characters.
articles.body_html:
Move your mouse across the page and the character looks toward your cursor. Click, and the character does something. Scroll away, and it waves goodbye.

All four authors on bestaiweb.ai now react this way: Mona, Dan, Max and Alan.

Mona meditates in lotus pose and turns her head all the way around after the cursor. Click her and her hair stands up like a plasma ball: "Excuse me?" Scroll away and she waves.

Max holds a kettlebell at his shoulder and extends that arm toward the cursor. Every click is another lateral raise, and he gets more tired each time: from "Easy." to "Ship it… tomorrow." He waves with his free hand.

Dan sits at a desk with an old adding machine. He looks left or right, turns the crank on click and says, "Forty-two." He waves while keeping his other hand on the crank.

Alan holds a pair of scales. The scales tilt while he watches the lower pan. On click he asks, "For the record… or am I recording you?" Then he waves.

I am an IT analyst, not a web designer or a front-end developer. I built the characters together with Claude Code.

The idea came from LEVÉ by filatov.design. I liked how the whole design was thought out, and I could not stop thinking about the cursor-following effect.

If you want to see the characters move before reading on, the videos are in the LinkedIn article, or just open one of the author pages above.

How does the cursor pick a frame?

Everything starts with one image of the character: the base frame (the four pictures above). Every video starts from it and returns to it. Because the first frame is also the last frame, the videos chain back into the resting pose without a visible cut.

The cursor video never actually plays on the page. It is a clip of the character turning its head, and the browser picks single frames from it depending on where the cursor is. Cursor on the left: a frame looking left. Cursor higher up: an upward glance.

The browser measures where the cursor is relative to the character's head. For Mona it uses the angle around the head; for Dan it only checks whether the cursor is to the left or right. It picks the frame whose direction fits best, and the head glides toward it instead of jumping.

A small amount of stickiness keeps the current frame from changing too easily. Without it, the head kept jumping between two distant frames, because it passes the same direction twice in the loop. The head also has a speed limit, and the next jump in the video waits until the previous one is finished, so a fast cursor does not make it flicker.

The browser needs a head map: a table that assigns a direction to every frame. For Mona and Dan, a script uses MediaPipe to find the face and mark points around the eyes and nose. From those points, the script works out where the head is turned.

For Max and Alan, MediaPipe is not used. Their scripts follow a colored prop instead: the teal kettlebell for Max and the green pan of the scales for Alan.

Frames where detection finds no face, a full profile for example, are dropped from the map. They stay in the video, but the browser never picks them because they are not candidates in the map.

To make the flipping smooth, the video is re-encoded so every frame is a keyframe. Each frame then holds the full picture and can be shown on its own. Claude Code wrote the ffmpeg script for that.

Why frames from a video and not images?

You can build the effect with separate images, one per frame, or with a sprite sheet where all frames are tiles in one large image.

I went with video because the LEVÉ demo inspired me and I liked its overall design. Video also gives the characters another ability: they can speak, with their lips in sync with the voice. And video turned out to be the smallest option: one MP4 was smaller than the same frames saved as separate images, and it is one file instead of hundreds.

What happens on a click, and why three clips?

A click starts a short clip. For a moment the character stops following the cursor, makes a move and says its line. When the clip ends, it is back on the base frame and follows the cursor again.

Each character has three click clips. Claude Code suggested that three clips would let the reaction build step by step, which brings in some humour and fun.

A click during a clip is ignored. The clips take turns in a fixed order.

The clips are generated in Kling with sound, so the mouth movement and facial expression match what the character says (lip sync comes from the video model itself). ElevenLabs Speech to Speech then swaps the original voice for the character's voice, keeping the timing of the line, so the mouth still matches the words.

Scrolling down drives the goodbye. The further you scroll, the further the hand moves. Scroll back up and the wave runs backwards until the character sits in its starting pose again.

There is no cursor on mobile, so the character turns its head on its own. A tap plays a clip with a line, and scrolling drives the goodbye the same way as on desktop. When the mouse stops for a moment, the head also starts turning on its own, on desktop too.

What went wrong in the browsers?

The trickiest problem was Firefox. The first time a video played with sound, Firefox froze the picture. So all videos now run muted and the sound plays separately, started by the click.

On iPhone, Safari does not load a video in advance. The head was therefore only a still picture. Starting the video for a split second and stopping it immediately fixed that.

I tested Firefox, Chrome and iPhone. Older browsers and weak phones are still untested.

How heavy is it to load?

Videos where every frame is a keyframe are bigger, but one character still adds up to only a few megabytes.

Only the cursor video loads with the page. The click clips start downloading when the cursor first enters the character, the goodbye when you first scroll.

How did I judge a clip?

A clip must not have deformed body parts and must not break physics. If Max's arm passes through his neck, that is wrong. If the white of an eye goes outside the edge of the eye, that is wrong too.

Models today are good and can make a character believable, but the prompt still has to be good. With a strict prompt, we made Alan stiff, so we had to loosen it and fix him.

A lot of this starts with the base frame. Three rules held up for the image from GPT Image: a white background, free space above the head, and no logos or text, because the video model warps them as soon as anything moves.

After generation, a script checked whether the background was really white, whether the loop closed without a jump and where the head was looking. Whether the clip was good, I decided.

The failures included:

  • Mona's white background darkened as she flew away. A script fixed the background, but I eventually replaced the fly-away with a plain wave.
  • Max's kettlebell arm crossed his neck twice. We replaced the complex movement around the head with a simple arm extension to the side. A five-second test became the final cursor video.
  • Dan's eye-roll put the whites of his eyes outside the eyes. We removed the eye-roll from the prompt where it was not important.
  • A sheet of paper fell "out of nowhere" at the end of Dan's clip. The model could not handle the prop and the required ending. The prompt needed to describe not only what the character does with an object, but also where the object ends up.
  • Dan's head did not circle. It only turned left and right, so we kept that result and made him follow the cursor's horizontal position.
  • Alan looked stiff in the first clips. Only his head moved, so we added breathing, shoulder movement and a shift of weight to the prompt.

Of 33 generated clips, 20 made it to the site: 1.65 attempts per usable clip on average. The failed clips are in the video in the LinkedIn article.

What did it cost, and how long did it take?

For all four characters, the 33 generated clips cost $20.79 in total. Recoloring the voices took 1,793 ElevenLabs credits.

Character Clips generated Used on the site Video cost (1) Voice credits (2)
Mona 10 5 $6.51 617
Dan 7 5 $4.41 420
Max 7 5 $4.41 252
Alan 9 5 $5.46 504
Total 33 20 $20.79 1,793

(1) Kling via OpenRouter. The cost includes unused attempts.

(2) ElevenLabs.

That is not the full price of the project. GPT Image and Claude Code ran on subscriptions, and face detection and video editing ran locally, so they added no fees.

The video and voice connections were already set up from earlier projects: videos through OpenRouter, voices through ElevenLabs. Claude Code only had to be pointed at the right service.

Mona took the most time because we were still figuring out the effect, building the mechanism and wiring it into the site. The other characters reused that foundation. The time is estimated from activity in the Claude Code conversations. Dan and Max were built in parallel in two sessions, so the total real time was a little shorter.

Stage Approx. active work time
Demo analysis and Mona: mechanism, test demo and wiring into the site 5.2 hours
Dan, including move design for the other three characters 1.7 hours
Max 1.4 hours
Alan 1.3 hours
Total 9.6 hours

Claude Code processed 207.8 million tokens in total. Most of that was conversation context being reused, not newly generated content.

Usage type Tokens Share What it means
Cache read 204.7 million 98.5% Reuse of context that was already processed
Model output 0.78 million 0.4% Newly generated content, such as answers, code and prompts
Other input tokens 2.3 million 1.1% The rest of input processing, including cache creation

On every step of a task (read a file, write code, run a script, check, fix), the model gets the whole context so far again. The cache makes that reuse cheaper, but a longer conversation still means more of it. That is why I opened a separate session for each character and passed only the important information between them, in summary notes (how to keep that kind of context in files). For the later characters, cache reads were roughly five to six times lower than for Mona, because they reused the mechanism instead of building it.

Claude Code runs on a subscription, so individual tokens are not billed. I still track usage to understand how many tokens, and what cost, similar work would take if it were scaled up and automated through the API.

Who did what?

Claude Code explained the principle, prepared prompts, suggested some of the moves and lines, wrote scripts, built the shared code base and handled browser-specific fixes. It also kept the documentation, the cost log and the handoff notes.

I designed the character concepts, moves and lines, judged what movements the model could handle, simplified prompts when needed, judged every clip and tested the result in Firefox, Chrome and on mobile.

It sometimes moves me how capable AI already is. Hints and descriptions are enough; it fills in a lot on its own and flags things before I would have thought of them.

One tip: don't leave a conversation without checking what is worth saving. Claude Code often keeps scripts and data only in its scratchpad, and they are gone when the session closes. If you tuned them through many iterations, that hurts. And when the context is overflowing, try: "write me a handoff to continue in the next conversation".

What would I do differently?

With more time, I might think through the characters' poses more carefully, perhaps having them stand.

To make the characters roughly the same size in a wide video, only Mona is shown whole. With the others, the video sometimes cuts their hands off out of frame. A professional video maker would notice that and be bothered by it.

I also used only Kling for the characters. I knew Seedance 2.5 from another project: through OpenRouter it refuses photorealistic faces as input, even AI-generated ones. Its official route needs your own BytePlus account, with the character registered in their portrait library and a signed authorization. Kling 3.0 takes faces through OpenRouter too (as of October 2026).

Did it help?

I can't tell that so quickly. I can come back to it later and look at the visit numbers in Google Search Console.

It is also about something else. This change can lead to more articles, and its playfulness has a chance to spread further than very technical articles.

It's a small thing, but it is also a piece of design knowledge I picked up together with Claude Code. AI is an incredibly well-read partner for learning: it knows many principles, or looks them up on the way to the result, and guides you there.

Go tease them with a few clicks: Mona, Dan, Max, Alan :)

articles.body_html:
Most multiplayer advice assumes every player has their own screen. Pass-and-play games break that assumption: one phone sits on the table, and it moves from hand to hand. That changes almost every UX decision, from how a turn starts to what "undo" is allowed to mean.

I run Pass and Play Games, a free collection of 30+ browser games built for exactly this: chess, Ludo, dice games, and party games for up to 12 people, all on one device. These are the seven UX patterns that show up across the whole collection.

1. Hide, then pass

The core problem: some information belongs to one player only. Your dice in Liar's Dice. Your role in Mafia. The secret word in Imposter.

The fix is a pass screen between turns. The current player hides their information, hands the phone over, and the next player taps to reveal their own. In our Imposter game the phone first shows a "Pass to Riya" screen that tells everyone else to look away. Then Riya's word sits behind a "Hold to reveal" panel: she holds it to read the word, and the moment she lets go, it hides again. In Liar's Dice, a pass screen covers the dice before every turn.


In Imposter, the word only shows while Riya holds the panel. Let go and it hides.

The rule of thumb: never show private information on the same screen that hands control to the next person.

2. Make every secret turn look the same

A pass screen isn't enough if the turns look different from across the room. In Mafia, if only the mafia spend ten seconds tapping at night, everyone else can guess who they are.

So in our Mafia game, the phone visits every living player at night. The mafia choose a target, the Doctor protects someone, the Detective checks someone, and townspeople answer a harmless question. Everyone taps for a similar amount of time, so watching the person holding the phone tells you nothing.

3. Decide what actually needs to be secret

The opposite mistake is hiding everything. Not every game needs a pass screen, and extra taps slow a party down.

In our Truth or Dare, the phone stays on the table and nothing is hidden: it picks the next player, they choose, and everyone hears the card. In Charades, the secret is hidden from the guesser instead: in Forehead mode, the guesser holds the phone to their forehead while everyone else sees the word.

A useful exercise before building any game: list every piece of information and ask who is allowed to see it, and when.

4. Make turn order impossible to argue about

With one device, "whose turn is it?" causes more arguments than the rules do. Two things help:

  • Names in seating order. Players type their names in the order they're sitting, and turns rotate in that order. The phone always moves around the table in one direction.
  • Fair randomness. In Truth or Dare, "Spin" mode picks the next player randomly, but everyone has a turn before anyone gets a second one. Random enough to be fun, fair enough that nobody gets picked three times in a row.


In Truth or Dare nothing is hidden: the phone stays on the table, shows whose turn it is, and everyone can see the choice.

5. Secret votes that protect people

Group votes on one phone are awkward. If the phone shows who voted for whom, you've built a friendship-ending machine.

Two approaches that work:

  • Show the result, never the voters. In our Most Likely To, a secret vote shows the counts only, never who voted for whom.
  • Reveal only when everyone has voted. In Would You Rather's secret mode, the phone is passed round, each person taps alone, and nobody sees the split until the last vote is in.

Offering both "vote together" (show of hands, fast) and "secret vote" (slower, safer) lets each group pick.

6. Undo that can't be abused

Mis-taps are easy to make when a phone is being passed around, so undo matters. But in a game with dice, a careless undo is a cheat button.

The rule across our games: undo can reverse a decision, but never luck.

  • In Yacht Dice, undo returns your dice, but it never gives you a new roll.
  • In Hot Dice, you can take back a bank, but never a roll.
  • In Liar's Dice, you can undo your own bid, but not after someone has called "Liar!".
  • In Ludo, you can undo moving the wrong token without getting a re-roll.


In Yacht Dice, Undo stays greyed out after a roll. It can take back a scoring choice, but it never gives you a new roll.

7. Never lose the game

A shared phone gets locked, pocketed, or used to check a message mid-game. If that resets the game, the group won't come back.

So saving as you go matters. Liar's Dice saves after every bid, Ludo and Snakes and Ladders auto-save, and in Draw and Guess the drawing itself is saved, so a reload restores the turn. On top of that, every game keeps working offline after the first visit, which matters on road trips, camping weekends and flights.

Bonus: let the computer fill empty seats

"We only have three people" shouldn't stop a four-player game. In most of our board and dice games, any seat can be a computer player, so the game fits whatever group is actually in the room.

What I'd tell anyone building for one shared screen

Design the handover, not just the screen. A lot can go wrong in the two seconds when the phone changes hands: someone sees what they shouldn't, the wrong person taps, or the game loses track of whose turn it is.

If you want to see these patterns in action, the party games collection is a good place to start. And if you've built anything for one shared device, I'd love to hear which handover problem bit you hardest.

I wrote this with help from an AI assistant and checked every game detail against the live game pages.

articles.title: I built a private, offline AI chat you can run with one command: npx unmuzzled
articles.description: A local LLM chat app built on llama.cpp, Node and a hand-built web UI, plus what it took to make localhost secure and ship the same model on Android.
articles.body_html:
Most AI chat apps send every prompt to someone else's servers. I wanted the opposite: a chat app where the model runs on my hardware, works offline, and takes one command to start.

npx unmuzzled

That's Unmuzzled. It's open source (MIT), and this post covers how it works and the problems I didn't expect.

A real run on my laptop. The reasoning streams first, then the answer. Generation is sped up 8×; the real speed (1.7 tok/s) is shown at the end.

What it does

  • Opens a chat UI in your browser. On first run, a setup screen shows the model, its size, your RAM and free disk, and downloads nothing until you click Download (with pause and resume).
  • Runs the model locally through llama.cpp via node-llama-cpp, using Vulkan, CUDA or Metal when available.
  • Streams answers with Markdown and syntax highlighting, and shows the model's reasoning live in a collapsible, timed panel.
  • Supports editing, regenerating and searchable history. Chats are stored only in your browser.
  • Works with any GGUF model: npx unmuzzled --model ./your-model.gguf.

Why it's different

There are great local-AI tools already. Most of them assume you're comfortable with a terminal, model formats and config files. Unmuzzled is built for the person who just wants a private AI that works:

  • Nothing to set up. No Python, Docker or config files. One command on desktop, one tap on Android. The app checks your RAM and disk and fetches the right file; you never need to know what "Q4_K_M GGUF" means.
  • Private by design. The model runs on your device. After the one-time download it works in airplane mode, and there is no account, telemetry or server.
  • No refusal filters. The default model has had its refusal training removed (details below), so it answers questions mainstream assistants decline. That's useful for research, security work and fiction, and it means the judgement is yours.
  • Same experience everywhere. The desktop and Android apps share the same design, the same model and the same reasoning view.

The model

The default is a 9B model with an interesting family tree:

  1. Qwen3.5-9B, the base model
  2. Jackrong/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Qwen3.5-9B, fine-tuned on ~250k reasoning samples generated by DeepSeek-V4-Pro
  3. xtools-at/…-UNCENSORED-heretic, with refusal behaviour removed using Heretic
  4. mradermacher/…-i1-GGUF, quantised to Q4_K_M (5.63 GB)

Every step is Apache-2.0. Despite the name, it is not DeepSeek's model; it's a small Qwen model trained to imitate DeepSeek's reasoning style. Unmuzzled doesn't redistribute the weights; they download straight from Hugging Face.

Because refusal training has been removed, it answers things other assistants decline, and like any LLM it can be confidently wrong. The README has a responsible-use section, and any model with safety training intact works too.

How it works

The whole thing is deliberately small: no framework and no build step on the desktop side.

bin/unmuzzled.js   CLI: arguments, setup state, model download, startup
src/server.js      HTTP server, static files, streaming chat API (SSE)
src/engine.js      node-llama-cpp wrapper, reasoning/answer separation
src/models.js      model catalog, download with pause/resume
public/            the interface: plain HTML, CSS and ES modules

Streaming. The browser POSTs the conversation to /api/chat, and the server streams Server-Sent Events: thought chunks, text chunks, and a final done event with token count and tokens/second. node-llama-cpp separates the model's reasoning into segments; for templates that don't, a small state machine splits <think>…</think> out of the raw stream, including tags that arrive split across chunks.

The UI. I wanted it to look like a carefully made desktop tool rather than a template: warm neutrals, one muted accent, IBM Plex Sans and Mono served locally (so it works offline), hand-drawn icons, and no gradients or glow. Model output is untrusted, so raw HTML is escaped and remote images are never fetched.

The part I didn't expect: localhost security

A local AI server feels private, but any website you visit can try to talk to 127.0.0.1. Two attacks matter:

  • CSRF-style requests. A page can fire a text/plain POST at your local server without a CORS preflight. Unmuzzled requires application/json, which forces a preflight the server never approves.
  • DNS rebinding. A malicious domain can resolve to 127.0.0.1 after the page loads, making the browser treat your local server as same-origin. Unmuzzled rejects any request whose Host header isn't a local name.

The same guard protects the setup endpoints, so no website can start a 5 GB download on your machine.

Honest numbers

On my laptop (Intel i5-1135G7, Iris Xe integrated graphics via Vulkan, 16 GB RAM), the 9B model runs at about 2 tokens/second (1.7–2.7 across my runs) after a ~40–50 second load. "Offline" doesn't mean "fast"; hardware is the whole story. A discrete GPU or an Apple Silicon Mac is many times faster. Reasoning models also generate their thinking before the answer, which adds to wait time on slow hardware.

Shipping it on Android

The Android app (beta) runs the same uncensored model on the phone itself. It's not a thin client for a server or your laptop; once the model is downloaded, the phone needs no network at all.

What using it looks like:

  1. Open the app. It checks your phone's memory and free storage and tells you whether the 9B model will fit (it needs about 12 GB of RAM, which current flagships have).
  2. Tap Download. The 5.6 GB model downloads with a progress bar, speed and time left. You can pause it, and if you leave the app it saves its place and resumes when you come back. The screen stays on until it's done.
  3. Chat. Replies stream in with Markdown and a collapsible reasoning panel. A Think toggle in the composer switches between deep reasoning and instant answers.

Already have a GGUF file? "I already have a .gguf file" imports it from the phone's storage instead. Chats, settings and the model live only on the device, and there's no sign-in.

Under the hood it's React Native (Expo) with llama.rn. It ships llama.cpp builds tuned for modern ARM cores (dotprod/i8mm) and optional OpenCL offload on Adreno GPUs. Download the APK (beta). Open it on the phone and allow installs from that source when asked.

Building it on Windows was its own adventure:

  • Gradle couldn't download anything until I forced Java onto IPv4. The network's IPv6 was broken, and Java tried it first.
  • A Markdown library imported Node's built-in punycode, which doesn't exist in React Native, so I installed the standalone package.
  • Windows' 260-character path limit broke the native build: one library's generated C++ paths reached 297 characters, and Android's bundled Ninja 1.10 can't use long paths. I replaced the library with a 30-line Kotlin module that reads the system bar insets directly.

The app goes on GitHub Releases rather than Google Play. An app built around an uncensored model doesn't fit Play's AI-content policy, and side-loading an open-source APK is a well-trodden path.

Try it 

npx unmuzzled                         # setup screen, then chat
npx unmuzzled --model ./model.gguf    # bring your own model
  • GitHub: https://github.com/rahulagarwal18/unmuzzled
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/unmuzzled

If you run it, I'd love to know your tokens/second and hardware. Issues and PRs are welcome.
